The traditional method for identifying intestinal parasites involves visual examination of a patient sample by a specialist, widely considered to be prone to inaccuracies due to potential inconsistencies and errors.  However, with the advancement of deep-learning-based image analysis techniques, it has become possible to enhance the reliability of visual diagnosis by substituting the expertise of a specialist with a complex artificial intelligence system.  In this study, we trained, tested, and applied a pre-existing deep learning model to a unique collection of images to assess its effectiveness in identifying intestinal parasites.  Our data consisted of 2469 images of five diverse species of parasites, gathered from 2469 samples of stool, which were collected from 1413 male and 756 female subjects, predominantly between the ages of 8 and 32.  The test involved comparing the performance of a pre-trained, state-of-the-art deep learning model with that of an experienced human diagnostician using three distinct sets of images.  The results revealed that the model, which employs a VGG16 architecture combined with attention and universal deep learning methods, demonstrates minimal bias toward the gender of subjects or their age groups.  Notably, it also achieves error rates significantly lower than those associated with human inspectors.  The study highlights the tremendous potential of deep learning to produce reliable diagnostic outcomes for a variety of medical conditions, while also reducing the risks of treatment-related errors.  Furthermore, the research shows that the model can successfully adapt to diagnose a broader spectrum of medical disorders, provided that a substantial body of relevant data is available for its training.  The study points out that the model can effectively substitute for the expertise of a specialist in visual inspection, effectively eliminating the likelihood of errors and consistent patterns of inadequacy associated with human evaluation.  In addition, the research finds that the deep learning model can successfully identify the presence of multiple parasites in samples, while imposing minimal computational burdens.  The study's findings are made publicly accessible in order to facilitate the development of more sophisticated artificial intelligence systems for parasite diagnosis in the future. This research focuses on understanding the characteristics of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and their host galaxies by using spectral energy distribution (SED) models to detect galaxy light. A dataset of 55 AGN from the XMM-COSMOS catalog at an observed z < 0.2 was selected, based on the availability of high-quality photometry data. By using the galaxy-light corrected fluxes, a comparison was made with the parent sample of the same objects. This revealed an increase in classification precision for AGN host galaxies at higher redshift intervals. Additionally, it was observed that the distribution of AGN blue host galaxies shifts from star-forming to passive with increasing redshift. However, a higher proportion of AGN host galaxies remain bluer than their non-AGN counterparts up to a redshift of 3. To investigate the causes behind AGN activity, we analyzed the mass-luminarity relations of galaxy pairs and found no indication of elevated masses in AGN host galaxies. Furthermore, we estimated the contribution of galaxy light to AGN fluxes, which ranged from 1 to 49% in low to high redshift intervals. In our analysis of AGN and galaxy correlations, we discovered AGN-galaxy correlations at lower redshift intervals but found them to be insignificant at higher redshift intervals (3 < z < 4) due to varying levels of noise. Overall, this research indicates that AGN play a minor role in the evolution of their host galaxies. We suggest representing an RGB image as a complex function with real and imaginary components corresponding to red and green colors and imaginary values representing blue. This complex representation enables various mathematical operations that can be translated into the RGB domain, resulting in novel and appealing images. Unlike other methods that mix colors by superimposing two images, our approach successfully blends multiple images by performing the average of complexes, thus retaining more color details. Additionally, we've found that our system naturally corrects hue shifts and creates a correlation between color channels. Consequently, we've developed six simple rules that leverage the symmetry and other properties of this system, resulting in six faithful image averaging algorithms. These rule-based approaches outperformed state-of-the-art baselines in a fair comparison and, not coincidentally, produced results comparable to extensive, manually-guided image editing. Furthermore, we've created a web-based interface that translates complex representations back to RGB images, allowing users to interact with and create new complex representations, and has already yielded new and exciting images. You can access this interactive platform at https://complex-images.github.io. A comprehensive collection of the generated images can be found at https://github.com/complex-images/wiki/dataset. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/complex-images. We have presented the theory and collected the resulting images in a dataset while this paper is under review with the aim of confirming our findings through audience feedback. Ultimately, we have made a significant contribution by opening a new area of research in image processing.

Our team has developed a class of quantum models, which we term Variational Quantum Models, that leverage variational and quantum computation for efficient evaluation and optimization. The circuit-based architecture of these models allows us to combine the strengths of classical and quantum processing units, specifically for problems involving $p$ parameters in the Pauli operators matrix. Importantly, our research highlights the significance of output choice in these models, showing that using the expectation value of quantum observables instead of energy yields optimized outcomes with reduced parameter choices, without the risk of local minima in the cost function. Furthermore, our models exhibit adaptable depth and entanglement, with the ability to adjust both variables according to the output choice. The research demonstrates the potential of Variational Quantum Models to serve as a universal framework for a wide array of quantum computing applications, encompassing tasks like simulation, estimation, search, and optimization on the quantum computer. A practical illustration of our models is provided by their successful application in solving the quantum time-evolution problem with impressive speed-up in comparison to classical methods for certain types of Hamiltonians. Our team has also experimented with variational quantum models as a substitute for the hybrid Monte-Carlo method, demonstrating the potential for substantial gain in efficiency, particularly for molecules with relatively small electronic correlation. The subject of coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering with a range of nuclei serves as a key area of research in current studies of particle physics. Contributions from nuclear modeling play a significant role in the analysis of this phenomenon. Our research provides a thorough examination of the CEvNS nuclear cross section predictions based on various nuclear models. A detailed comparison of the predicted cross sections is offered for 152 nuclei, ranging from hydrogen to lead, and for several prominent experiments including the COHERENT, Adam, and CLIO. The distinction between the cevns.scatter Python library, which is based on single-nucleon calculations, and the cevns.kinetic package, which considers the collective nuclear behavior, is explored in depth. An additional goal of our research is to evaluate the accuracy of current CEvNS cross section predictions and to address discrepancies between experimental data and the cevns.scatter predictions for the CLIO experiment. To facilitate future work, our research is presented as a open-source Python framework allowing for CEvNS cross section predictions to be computed with a variety of nuclear models. This framework is capable of producing detailed reports of cevNS cross section predictions for specified experiments and nuclei. Furthermore, our research outlines a simple analysis for evaluating the accuracy of cevNS cross section predictions. This analysis compares single-nucleon and collective nuclear models, which are characterized by significantly different levels of accuracy. A summary of the cevNS data quality criteria is provided for over 70 nuclei, allowing for the straightforward identification of data considered reliable, marked in red, and unreliable, marked in blue. This research is currently in preparation for publication in the journal Physical Review C. A two-point error gauge is commonly employed in such cases to evaluate the error distribution of CMB maps. This paper provides a statistical model that defines the two-point error gauge's behavior in relation to point sources that are either weak or extremely strong. According to this model, the error distribution of CMB maps featuring strong point sources is likely to be non-uniform, resulting in an overestimation of the two-point error gauge's value. The error model takes into consideration the specific shapes of Gaussian templates used to remove the strong point sources and the scanner's systematic noise. This research explores the long-term behavior of solutions to a given class of time-periodic parabolic equations, which seek to minimize an energy function with random initial conditions. The studies reveal that solutions converge to the equilibrium set of undriven systems in cases with widespread initial outbreaks, but reach a different equilibrium in areas where the initial presence is limited. The analysis takes into account the degree of disorder and intensity of the disordering force. The findings are verified through numerical examples. The equilibrium set of these time-periodic equations is comprised of periodic solutions whose growth is either accelerating or slowing down. The studies of homogenization and Hamilton-Jacobi equations provide essential background for this research. The undriven energy limit is described through a reduced Hamilton-Jacobi equation, which offers insight into the behavior of the running average of the first integral of the disordering force. The analysis considers two scenarios: the disordering force and its effect for large and small values of the disordering parameter. The studies of homogenization reveal that in the limit where the disordering parameter goes to infinity, the first integral's limit is either -∞ or doesn't change as the disordering parameter increases. The phase portrait of the running averages' limit is thus dependent on the variation of the disordering parameter and its effect, while the beginning points of the limits are described through the first integral's Hamilton-Jacobi equation. The findings indicate that the limits of the equilibrium sets of the driven and undriven systems differ generally, but converge under specific conditions. The studies explore the degree of disorder and intensity of the disordering force's effect in the periodic solutions' equilibrium set. The analysis reveals that the limits of the periodic solutions' equilibrium set are not only highly disordering-dependent but also show varying behavior based on the disordering parameter's limit, which may lead to the emergence of various patterns in the periodic solutions equilibrium set in the limit of homogenization. The studies of homogenization consider an all-time limit scenario of the driven system's energy's limit, which offers a one-dimensional simplified model description. The research finds that the models' behavior can be similar not only in the models themselves but also in the models' background equations for large values of the disordering parameter's limit. Many unsupervised speech synthesis approaches have produced impressive results,
yet it remains unclear how their quality compares to supervised systems. To address
this gap, we present an unsupervised speech synthesis system that generates new
utterances from existing ones without manual label marking. We compare its
output, represented as a distribution over possible utterances, to the product of
two supervised distributions, one derived from speech and the other from text.
We evaluate and analyze the quality of synthesized speech using various metrics
and applications, including the mean opinion score, as well as metrics such as
word error rate and short sentence improvement. The results indicate that the
unsupervised system produces utterances that are 4% less intelligible than those
generated by a supervised system, according to the mean opinion scores from a
human evaluation. However, the difference in quality is significantly smaller when
measured using the short sentence improvement metric, which assesses the quality of
synthesized speech at a higher level of granularity. We investigated the possible
explanations for the discrepancy between the human evaluations and the objective
metrics by inspecting the characteristics of the synthesized utterances. The
synthesized utterances from the unsupervised system exhibit fewer errors in speech
and have more natural distributions of phonemes, parts of speech, and word
sequences, which surpass those of the supervised system. Interestingly, while
both systems fall short of matching the accuracy of human speech, they excel in
specific areas where humans struggle. For instance, the unsupervised system
excels in generating sequences of words that are unlikely to occur in real life,
whereas the supervised system outperforms it in reproducing accurate pronunciations
of spoken words. Overall, the research suggests that the quality of the
synthesized speech from the unsupervised system approaches that of its supervised
counterpart in multiple aspects under various evaluation methods. We argue that
further advancements in this area are plausible and that the current output from
the unsupervised system already surpasses human capabilities in several tasks. 
Despite the progress made, there are still several tasks where the unsupervised
system continues to underperform relative to its supervised counterpart. 
Consequently, there exists significant potential for future improvement in
future research endeavors. To facilitate future exploration, we present a dataset
designed for comparison, comprising the output from the unsupervised and supervised
systems as well as the corresponding original utterances. The dataset has been
made publicly available at https://github

In synthetic differential geometry, the source path and groupoid are crucial concepts, and a path is considered part of a given groupoid if it's consistent with its source and target aspects. A specifically defined geometric groupoid, featuring a distinguished point called the point at infinity, is crucial in this area of study. It's well established that such a groupoid can be broken down into associated rings based on the point at infinity. We provide conditions under which a source path consistent with a given groupoid results in the path being consistent with its source and target aspects under a related ring's action. We then use this breakthrough to establish the action of geometric groupoids on their respective rings in a generalized form, ultimately contributing to the advancement of synthetic differential geometry. We apply these findings to examine the properties of differential modules and their relationship with the action of geometric groupoids on their associated rings, resulting in the identification of novel differential modules derived from a given path, along with the demonstration of their connection to earlier work in this field. We further use these results to establish the action of geometric groupoids on their associated rings in a new light, revealing that the identified action aligns with the conventional action defined in earlier work, and then proceed to establish the correspondence between paths consistent with a given groupoid and the closed differential modules adapted from a geodesic interval. Our final step involves providing geodesic descriptions of paths consistent with a given groupoid, resulting in a significant finding in the field. We believe that our collection of new results will significantly contribute to the understanding of path concepts in synthetic differential geometry. By the nature of our work, we provide geodesic descriptions of paths consistent with a given groupoid based on its geometric properties rather than additional postconditions. Additionally, our path descriptions demonstrate adaptability across various geometric groupoids and their corresponding rings, showcasing the versatility of our approach. We leverage the capabilities of category theory to achieve a seamless flow of reasoning across the various mathematical entities involved in our research. We begin by introducing novel geometric groupoids and their resulting rings, followed by the establishment of correspondence between paths and differential modules, and then derive the description of paths consistent with a given groupoid through the adaptation of geodesic intervals. We establish analogous results specific to the non-geometric setting, providing a deeper understanding of path concepts in this area. In February 2021, the Dynaswap project launched a decentralized, Swiss-based blockchain-based e-voting system. Following this, an attack was carried out on the Dynaswap testnet in April of the same year, which not only undermined the system but also exposed serious security flaws. This research paper presents a comprehensive investigation of the assault on Dynaswap, including how the attackers manipulated specific smart contracts and used compromised private keys to steal Ethereum tokens and trigger failed transactions. Furthermore, the paper outlines a series of security measures and countermeasures aimed at enhancing the Dynaswap platform's security, including integration of additional security tools such as hotp, reentrancy protection, immutable log storage, and fail-fast mechanisms. Lastly, the paper discusses the potential implications and consequences of the detected vulnerabilities in the context of the Dynaswap production environment and future political elections. With a focus on educational and theoretical aspects, the paper offers these security measures as recommendations for potential users of the Dynaswap platform. The paper concludes by highlighting lessons that can be learned from the Dynaswap assault and proposes relevant courses of action. These measures not only apply to Dynaswap but can also be adopted by the broader blockchain and general software development communities. The Dynaswap project's critical assessment is carried out by Michiel Van Lim, with Thierry Redant and Benoit Vienne contributing to the examination of technical details. As of June 2021, the Dynaswap project has ceased its activities. Despite this, the research presented in this paper remains relevant and prescriptive, with a focus on Dynaswap specifically but also applicable to the broader blockchain realm. The paper's conclusions based on factual data do not express a personal opinion. In 2021, the paper's main findings were shared with the Dynaswap project's team. This research explores the performance of a secure multiuser communication system that incorporates reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) to manage the effects of hardware impairments under optimal conditions. The study assumes that the minimum rate of transmission for each user is known, and all devices have access to channel state information. An optimization problem is created to maximize the total data rate, which is calculated as a combination of the rates for each user, subject to constraints based on the minimum required rates and hardware impairment. The formulation of this optimization problem involves nonconvex equations and inequalities, which are addressed through an alternating optimization algorithm that uses the Z-quadratic optimization technique and the Marquardt algorithm. With this method, the researchers were able to reduce the optimization problem to two simpler subproblems per iteration and increase the total data rate by 70% compared to the baseline in the presence of severe hardware impairments. The efficiency of this method was also verified by reducing the computational time by 50% when compared to the baseline. The results show that the proposed algorithm offers a balance between system performance and computational efficiency. The impact of hardware impairments on the total data rate is quantified as a function of the power control accuracy and the RIS power, and the study reveals that the effect of hardware impairments on the system can be mitigated by adjusting the RIS power. The total data rate is found to increase as the RIS power increases and the hardware impairment exponent decreases. The researchers also discovered relationships between the average power control and the hardware impairment exponent as well as the number of RIS elements. The validity of this model is proven through simulation results. A fairness analysis is then presented to assess how the proposed algorithm affects the rate distribution among users. The study reveals that the rate distribution is impacted by the presence of hardware impairments, but the effect can be mitigated by adjusting the RIS power. The total data rate fairness is found to decrease as the RIS power increases, which is an expected result. The researchers then presented methods to increase the total data rate fairness by adjusting the RIS power and the data transmission time. The impact of hardware impairments on the system is quantified as a function of the power control accuracy and the number of users, and the study reveals that the effect of hardware impairments on the system can be mitigated by adjusting the RIS power and the data transmission time. Building upon the insights of systems like ANS and WAS, we propose an innovative method for using was-like algorithms in a more efficient manner: instead of constantly generating attention maps, we suggest focusing on developing a vocabulary of was-like algorithms that can anticipate and address challenging aspects of a given learning sequence. 

These anticipated problem-solving tools, dubbed 'hindsight summaries', are predicted prior to making predictions with the entire sequence. They are based on the understanding that certain systems, designed in advance, can tackle specific learning challenges more effectively. Hypothesically, a sequence learner with access to these summaries is likely to experience reduced error rates over time, particularly as their own vocabulary and library of was-like algorithms expand. 

To test this idea, we explored the ANS algorithm's ability to make sense of the Past Event Bank, as proposed in Was. However, instead of learning an event bank from scratch, we discovered that the ANS algorithm can generate more accurate results if it only considered a limited, previously known set of past experiences. 

In line with our hypothesis, providing the ANS algorithm with a limited set of past experiences allows it to anticipate and address more complex events more effectively, ultimately producing less inaccurate 10-year-old recall in certain domains. These summaries are then used to create a new was-like algorithm - WASm. Finally, we close with a reflection on the broader implications of this new was-like algorithm, WASm.

The source of kinetic energy for solar wind is still the subject of ongoing research. Researchers have long assumed a smooth, continuous distribution of energy, but recent studies at 1 AU and other points along the solar system's radial structure suggest a dual-source model would be more accurate. These findings, which were published in a previous paper, show a clear distinction in the kinetic energy density's distribution at 1 AU and indicate a change in its origin. In a conventional optical system, the application of a magnetic field transforms the Hamiltonian into a form related to the Dirac equation with a built-in Kerr nonlinearity. By incorporating an optical cavity and applying an electromagnetic field to the system, it exhibits characteristics of both optomechanics and Rabi coupling. In an alternative approach, we introduce the concept of 'deformed' optomechanics without incorporating additional photons, instead using a single Rabi coupling, to observe distinct effects on the system's spectrum and entanglement. The spectrum shows typical optomechanic features in the weak-tunneling limit, however, in the strong-tunneling limit, it displays an intense and broadened absorption peak, with the associated probe-field decrease prevented by a balance achieved through tunelling and optomechanical strengths. We also study the entanglement between the two levels and find that its magnitude solely relies on the optical cavity's quantum characteristics, specifically, the Rabi coupling and deformed frequencies. The presence of 'dark states', within the which the entanglement attains a maximum, is discovered and investigated in detail. The incorporation of 'deformed' optomechanics offers a simple method to create states with nonlinear characteristics through tunability of the tunneling and optomechanical couplings. It is worth noting that a 'deformed' optomechanic can be considered as the quantum mechanical equivalent of a q-deformed harmonic oscillator, however, in the context of a q-deformed optical system, the entanglement shows a more complex dependence on the q-deformation parameter in comparison to the optomechanic system studied here. The system studied here is found to demonstrate 'deformed' optomechanic characteristics even in the presence of Brownian motions, however, in a future study, we intend to investigate its behavior under this specific condition. The observed transition strengths with regard to energy are significantly lower than those of the R-positive scissors modes, leading to the conclusion that the localised nature of the R-negative states does not prevent their interaction with the scissors degrees of freedom. Furthermore, the relationship between the R-negative states and the beta scissors mode is supported by the observation of a clearly defined energy spectrum, in addition to the mixing between the $K$ wave functions characteristic of deformed rotors, indicating degeneracy in the $K$-bands. The findings are consistent with the concept of a deformation parameter as proposed in the shell-model-like approach to the nuclear scissors mode. The presence of strength in the electromagnetic transition to the 2$^{+}$ scissors mode, in addition to the known transition to the 3$^{-}$ state, has also been observed, and we suggest that this 2$^{+}$ state can be identified as the straightforward mixture of the gamma vibration and the gamma-deformed state, resulting in a parameter-free mixing. The absence of experimental data for electromagnetic transition rates to the low lying negative states in $^{120}$Sm, in contrast to our theoretical calculations which demonstrate significant strengths, suggests these states could be identified as a distinct phenomenon different from the conventional R-negative states. The distinct nature of these states can be explored by analysing the pattern of electromagnetic transition strengths to the negative states, which appears to be a superposition of patterns associated with quasiproton and neutron R-negative states, in addition to the characteristics of deformed states in the neighbourhood of the neutron and proton closed shells.

A key part of understanding text is extracting the specific events it's describing along with the roles those involved. Current methods used for this task, known as Event Extraction, are highly dependent on trained models, yet they often struggle when applied to languages other than English. Since these models aren't available for non-English languages, a common practice has become to translate text into English and perform Event Extraction there. Our research aims to change this by developing an EEE system tailored for the Spanish language. To achieve this, we've assembled a dataset of Spanish texts similar to those used in English for Event Extraction, and we've also compared our system's performance to that of a model that performs text translation. Our results indicate that, generally, translating the text yields better outcomes, yet when working directly with the original language yields comparable if not superior results. Additionally, our contributions include the creation of a reliable Spanish Event Extraction dataset that allows for a direct comparison of how the task is performed in that language. Our research code and this dataset are now openly accessible. The former enables researchers to leverage our approach, which uses pre-trained modules for NLP, a more recent advancement in this field. The latter, our Spanish Event Extraction dataset, is unique in its accuracy and comprehensive coverage of 1,315 distinct event types. These events are part of 13 distinct categories of scenarios in which they occur. The dataset consists of 13k root verbs signaling the start of specific events and their respective arguments. These arguments have been categorized into approximately 30 distinct groups. The dataset, known as SpastEE, is composed of nearly 231k sentences extracted from news articles in 2019 and 2020, and from scholarly publications in 2016 and 2017. The accuracy of SpastEE has been verified through multiple rounds of data refinement in which human evaluators analyzed a selected subset of the data for accuracy. The findings of these evaluations have been incorporated into the dataset through an automatic re-evaluation of the data's annotations. The results have shown that SpastEE is on par with similar datasets for English (SemEval-2015 Task 11) and Arabic (MOODS 2016), offering significantly more detailed and accurate annotations. The results have shown the accuracy of SpastEE is higher than that of datasets for English and Arabic likely due to the limitations of translating text from other languages and to the quality of SpastEE itself. Our work in \citet{rosenberg-loupp2020} demonstrated that a combined model of syntax and semantics, trained on synthetic data, developed consistent with Turkle's hypothesis. This involved analyzing the relationship between verb phases and the structural phases of the syntactic tree in phase-based grammars. In the current study, we expanded this research by examining whether the observed patterns in a joint model of syntax and semantics are present in actual languages spoken by native speakers. To this end, we developed a phase-based grammar for Japanese and utilized it to generate synthetic sentences that test the effects of verb phase alignment on sentence meaning. Subsequently, we conducted an online study to gather ratings from native Japanese speakers regarding the synthesized sentences. The study revealed that Japanese speakers, like the models we trained, tend to conjoin sentences that have the same structural phases as the verbs governing them, aligning with Turkle's hypothesis. Furthermore, we observed that the synthesized sentences were rated similarly to genuine ones in terms of acceptability ratings, indicating that the joint model accurately captured the underlying syntactic-semantic connections in Japanese. In addition to these findings, we discovered evidence of phase-based semantics in Japanese, which were absent in the initial model training. Ultimately, our studies indicate that the joint models we trained successfully captured both the patterns seen in synthetic data and the real-world language being studied. Thus, our research suggests that the joint models are effective tools for analyzing and understanding the complex interplay between syntax and semantics in human languages. The Azimuthally symmetric Theory of Gravitation seeks to address the Radiation Problem encountered in massive star formation by accounting for gravitational effects on surrounding accretion disks and jets as they emit electromagnetic radiation. This research develops a comprehensive model, incorporating both thermal and non-thermal energy sources, which can be used to simulate high-energy processes associated with massive star formation. This approach, in the context of the initial model, indicates that electromagnetic radiation emitted by the accretion flow may be scattered in an isotropic pattern before reaching the outer environment, thus explaining the observed absence of intense gamma-ray emissions from specific star formation sites. Consequently, a modified version of the model is considered, which includes the redirection of gamma-rays within the disk, resulting in an anisotropic radiation pattern. The rapid changes in fast radio bursts, particularly their scattering properties, remain poorly understood due to a lack of synchronized observations that can constrain emission theories. Until now, radio interferometry has been the primary method for observing these transient events as their spectral and scattering characteristics offer clues about their surroundings. This study presents a novel approach using a synchronized observing technique to observe FRBs in real-time across multiple radio frequencies, thereby enabling the precise measurement of their scattering properties. The path to implementing this approach involves contributing to an open source radio interferometry library called radio-astropy, which we used to generate sample observation results at the time of this study. The adoption of synchronized observing practices could significantly enhance our understanding of FRB science, particularly the radio radiation process, while observations of FRB additional phenomena (such as lenths, periodicity, and localization) could offer new insights into its origins. Ultimately, the detection of 19 FRCs (FRB-like events) within this study may signify the emergence of a previously undefined astrophysical source category distinct from known FRB categories. This paper presents a innovative approach to enhancing the modeling of viscoelasticity in solid mechanics through continued learning. By capitalizing on the 'if-adapter' strategy from the field of computer vision, our method efficiently uses historically accurate predictions to minimize the impact of future prediction inaccuracies. To alleviate the challenges of future prediction, our model automatically identifies and focuses on readily predictable outcomes. This data-efficient strategy is effective in modeling complex processes like hyper-viscocity, which have complex temporal dependencies. By refining our model's ability to retain memory and improve the prediction of its initial stages, our results show that we can achieve up to a 34-fold improvement in the model's performance. This breakthrough allows us to validate the 'if-adapter' strategy in the field of solid mechanics, which has a range of practical applications. With the ability to train our models on inherently noisy data, our method also includes a noise-filtering mechanism to ensure data quality. By achieving improved results with less data, our approach contributes to the continued learning trend in the field of solid mechanics. This analysis found that the $epsilon(10753)^{+}$ coupling to the operator $(cs)$, which corresponds to the diquark-antidiquark picture, is significantly smaller at around $0.56\cdot10^{-2}$, in contrast to the coupling to the operator $(c\sphericalOmega s)$, which is much larger at approximately $1.56\cdot10^{-2}$. As a result, the analysis provides minimal evidence for the intermediate state $(c\sphericalOmega s)$ in the process $b\bar b \to epsilon(10753)^{+}$ and indicates that the $epsilon(10753)^{+}$ has a very small contribution from the $1D_{2}^{1}$ component. Consequently, a level shift of $0.12^{+0.04}_{-0.03}$ MeV was added to the $1D_{2}^{1}$ mass in the strong coupling analysis, which resulted in a revised mass of $11057\pm 14$ MeV. The analysis further determined that the angular momentum between the quark and antiquark in the $epsilon(10753)^{+}$ is likely $l=1$ and assigned the state to $1^{3}D_{1}^{+}$. The development of askesngd began as a complementary resource for the SimPy library, focusing on streamlining the process of simultaneous training and simulation of deep neural networks with a high level of configurability. AskewSGD supports the optimization of deep neural networks with various loss functions, learning rate schedules, and quantization protocols. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of implementing a quantized neural network training workflow using AskewSGD on GPUs, similar to conventional non-Spiking deep neural networks. Compared to the conventional method, AskewSGD achieves a significant 2.5-fold speed boost. An in-depth overview of AskewSGD's architecture, as well as its practical applications in both Spiking-Deep-Spiking and Spiking-Non-Spiking settings, is provided. AskewSGD achieves a satisfactory performance in Spiking-Non-Spiking precision compared to the conventional approach, with results within 2% of the state-of-the-art accuracy achieved by conventional methods on similar datasets. AskewSGD also surpasses existing benchmarks in Spiking-Non-Spiking accuracy while utilizing Spiking-Deep-Spiking as the teacher, resulting in a significant speed boost of 3.7 times. These labels have several useful applications and are a key structure in various graph knowledge extraction problems. A significant open question has been whether fault-tolerant distance labels can be constructed for all graphs in a graph with maximum degree Δ, with a bound of O(log |G| / log log |G|). A new approach for identifying distinct brain regions in MRI scans utilizes Gaussian Processes to model variations in scan values, enabling precise segmentation of major brain areas. To improve the limited information obtained from individual scans, we developed a non-parametric Bayesian model that combines data from multiple scans within a hierarchical framework. This model has the added benefit of naturally handling missing data, allowing for its application to multi-modal and multi-timepoint analyses. Through our experiments, we established the robustness of our approach by comparing it with established methods using established gold-standard training datasets and also demonstrated its performance using the open-source HCP dataset. This work will form the basis for a wider investigation into the application of non-parametric Bayesian models in medical imaging. A Python implementation of the code is available for public access at the link https://github.com/twinger/sgpHierarchicalGP.git. 

Keywords: Gaussian Processes, Bayesian Hierarchies, MRI Scanning, Machine Learning, Machine Learning in Medicine.

We investigate the interplay between dissipation and Floquet heating in a one-dimensional Bose gas confined to a weakly coupled chain linked to a heat bath. The boundary interaction with the heat bath is kept minimal, yet sufficient to significantly impact the gas's thermal behavior. Under Floquet driving, the system undergoes Floquet heating, characterized by a substantial increase in energy due to minimal dissipation, and subsequently, the system's low-frequency dynamics are governed by nonlinear Floquet theories. Conversely, high-frequency phenomena are regulated by linear Floquet modes, which linearly shift with frequency. We discover a nonlinear phase shift involving Floquet heating, where initial Floquet excitations are produced and mature, leading to the formation of a Bose condensation, which is linked to periodic energy density fluctuations. Moreover, we find an insulating phase, marked by boundary Floquet heating, which causes dissipation at the boundaries, thereby reducing mobility. Employing a two-site model, we extensively examine the insulating phase's behavior and its transition to the Floquet heating phase. Using the Floquet-Matveyesyan-Kotliar-Jáuregui model, we determine various system parameters, and via this computational approach, we determine critical temperatures, related to Bose condensation, as well as their dependence on driving frequency. Finally, we explore an alternative insulating state, which arises from dissipation-induced self-trapping, and discuss the intricate interplay between the two types of insulating states and Floquet heating phases. Upon enhancing dimensionality via DMRG simulations, we observe a phase transition from the insulating to Floquet heating phase, and find Floquet heating occurs in one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems with the emission of low-energy collective excitations as prototypical Floquet photons. Moreover, these simulations reveal a C-Fermi liquid behavior in a one-dimensional system, which links to a Fermi gas due to long-distance degeneracy caused by photon emission. However, these simulations stop short at the 1D-2D boundary transition because of the emergence of massless collective excitations. Further Investigations are needed to take the system into the 2D-3D region. If Floquet heating occurs in three-dimensional systems remains an open question, which is an active area of research at the moment. Research into optical clocks based on two-level quantum systems, including rubidium and aluminium, has revealed the crucial influence of photodetection on their operation. In the case of optical clocks based on a three-level system (e.g. enriched $^{87}$Rb), the photodetection process can create unwanted complex dynamics, originating from the absorption and emission of photons in the metastable excited states. This study investigates the impact of photodetection on the complex dynamics of enriched $^{87}$Rb and explores possible methods to suppress these effects. We discover that in cases with low photon absorption compared to emission, the complex dynamics can be comprehensively described by a simple analytical model, revealing a time-varying density matrix that can be expressed as a combination of exponential functions. In addition, we identify suitable conditions to suppress the unwanted complex dynamics in enriched $^{87}$Rb, making it possible to eliminate the associated systematic errors in quantum logic-based applications. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be adapted to other similar systems, including the chemically enriched $^{144}$Sm. In the case of low photon absorption, the complex dynamics can be modelled as a pure dephasing process with time-varying characteristics, directly linked to the time-varying optical participation ratio. In the studies examined, the logical application of enriched $^{144}$Sm appears to be safe from the complex dynamics effect. The study yields deeper insights into the causes of pure dephasing in cases without external magnetic fields, linking the phenomenon to the optical participation ratio. The research also identifies the possibility of eliminating the complex dynamics effect through reduced optical density matrices. The demonstrated methodology provides Enriched $^{87}$Rb and the potentially chemically enriched $^{144}$Sm with the necessary complexity requirements for quantum logic applications, achieving accuracy within a few seconds beyond the photon absorption time. The complex dynamics effect in other similar systems can be assessed using the model developed and the associated tools, enabling simulations for a range of optical powers. The study further proposes methods to minimize the complex dynamics effect through reduced optical density matrices. The developed approach makes enriched $^{87}$Rb and the potentially chemically enriched $^{144}$Sm suitable candidates for quantum logic applications with accuracy within a few seconds beyond the photon absorption time. The widespread employment of Deep Neural Networks (DNN) in approximate nearest neighbor search, particularly in image retrieval tasks, has been proven very effective. A prominent method known as Wide-Attention Network (WAN) excels in image retrieval, achieving exceptional results. In our research, we investigate the inherent properties of the training process of WAN and identify two crucial gradients components that significantly influence the final outcome after backpropagation. By decomposing the gradient of pair-wise loss, we create a revised training algorithm, enhancing WAN's performance further. The improved method, dubbed Multi-Gradient WAN, demonstrates superior evaluation metrics across various benchmarks, comprising the widely accepted MS-Coco and MS-MSCO and the medical-specific Galvani-X-Ray and Galvani-Sim. MG-WAN achieves superior results, with evaluation metrics surpassing WAN's performance, with significant improvements of 8% or more on the Galvani-X-Ray and Galvani-Sim datasets and 2-3% on MS-Coco and MS-MSCO. The improved method, MG-WAN, also outperforms the two-year-old WAN baseline, showcasing its robustness and stability across time. Moreover, MG-WAN's evaluation metrics significantly surpass the state-of-the-art methods, including BN-Softmax WAN and RFB-ANNO WAN, while demonstrating superior computational efficiency and architectural simplicity in comparison to the latter methods. The improved method, Multi-Gradient WAN, also demonstrates very competitive results on the standard ImageNet dataset. Text messages can be erased due to error-prone or accidental deletion, but a dedicated "delete" button is not provided on our phones, although it's a crucial option. Historically, the physical world lacked similar mechanisms to erase data; however, this changed with the introduction of quantum teleportation, allowing for the erasure of quantum states via classical communication. Our discussion will focus on general corrections for quantum states, discovering that any correction involving a single type of tensor necessitates a specific type of tensor network - an isotropic 2D lattice - and that certain degrees of freedom can't be modified without introducing conflicting operations, implying the need for customized corrections depending on the state to be corrected. A specific example illustrates these findings, involving a qubit connected to a 4-qubit Bell-diagonal state. An efficient, local correction for this state doesn't exist; therefore, we'll describe a method to erase this state while mimicking the effect of deleting a message on a 2D lattice and demonstrating its practical application in a real-world scenario, effectively converting an incompatible correction for the qubit alone into an acceptable correction for the entire Bell-diagonal state. These discussions will provide an innovative understanding of data deletion, introducing novel concepts, such as deleting entire information-theoretic units, and offering unique perspectives on established concepts, such as quantum teleportation, which, despite its name, can serve as an information-erasure mechanism. In multi-armed bandits, we have examined non-stochastic projects where the qualities of the arms shift arbitrarily with no discernible pattern. Based on assumptions about the arm qualities and gaps between them, we derived regret bounds under two different models - one where the best arm's decline can be significant and another where it's limited. In the first model, we allowed for substantial declines in the best arm's value, but imposed a moderate limit on how much it might drop. This led to regret bounds with a logarithmic component related to the number of steps and a poly logarithmic component related to the number of arms. In the second model, assuming the gaps between the arm values are substantial and the declines in the best arm's value are proportionally small, we derived a regret bound with poly algebraic components involving the number of arms, steps, missing arm values, declines in the best arm's value, declines in other arm values, and the reciprocal of the gaps between the arm values. These findings also provide estimates for situations with multiple optimal arms. All the derived regret bounds hold a poly logarithmic factor. Based on these results, we can estimate the number of steps needed to achieve a desired level of confidence in our estimation. We also presented a model to calculate the expected time needed for optimal arm identification. This research extends the existing bounds by generalizing the conditions for identifying the optimal arm. We established tighter regret bounds under the initial model's assumptions. We also identified two specific scenarios where arm identification methods based on exploration can fall short - one with extremely small gaps between the arm values and another with arbitrary gaps and a limited number of arms. In these two scenarios, we demonstrated the superiority of scheduling methods over traditional exploration approaches. This research explores the optimal arm identification in a variety of settings - multi-armed bandits, direct optimization, and scheduling, identifying common themes and contrasts among the different models. However, current approaches limit the complexity of these models to improve performance and reliability. We introduce a new theoretical framework for text generation that enables rapid exploration of the language space without compromising quality, by representing each possible text through multiple interconnected vectors. The framework's parameters are trained to ensure generated texts meet the requirements of a given task, while also being similar to existing texts. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach in a dataset of dialogues, where the optimization of a single parameter leads to substantial improvements in performance and overall text quality. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that the similarity relationships induced within the model outperform those achieved through traditional language models. Since its inception more than 50 years ago, a crucial aspect of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) has been left unexplored - how matter is formed in high-energy collisions. This review explores non-equilibrium QCD, focusing on how a hot QCD plasma is created at moderate coupling strengths. Plugging in current experimental data, we examine the feasibility of achieving this plasma at the LHC and future RHIC experiments. Ultimately, we outline the key goals and challenges of a new research program aimed at understanding the plasma's precursor state. This program could be facilitated by cutting-edge experiments at existing facilities, complemented by advanced theoretical studies. By pursuing this program, we can significantly boost our understanding of QCD and the plasma's behavior in a predetermined state. This review is based on a comprehensive series of lectures, 'New Horizons in a Hot QCD Plasma', delivered at the Galileo Galilei Institute in Pisa, Italy. The review consists of six articles, with the current abstract serving as the first installment. The complete series is included in this repository as an alternative to printed volumes. The current abstract is available as arXiv:2203.03414. The complete series can be found as ar arXiv:2203.03416, with individual installments as ar arXiv:2203.03415,2203.03417,2203.03418,2203.03419, and 2203.03420. The moving-stable approach offers a practical method for modeling the impact of stochastic elements, such as turbulence and wave patterns, on offshore wind turbine structures. This method converts time-varying stochastic processes into a series of steady, uniform wind and wave conditions, corresponding to various levels of turbulence intensity. A case study off the coast of Portugal found that incorporating stochastic variability provided a more accurate representation of structural loads, often increasing the design loads by up to 20% compared to a purely deterministic model. However, the added uncertainty in the model did not translate to equivalent variations in the predicted fatigue damage of the offshore wind turbines. Factors such as wave patterns and turbulence intensity were found to significantly affect the variability of structural loads, whereas wave direction and wind direction were found to have a minimal impact. Lastly, incorporating stochastic variability using the moving-stable approach resulted in a computational cost reduction of two orders of magnitude compared to a traditional Monte-Carlo simulation. This method facilitates the integration of stochastic variability into high-resolution simulations of offshore wind turbines, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of their dynamic behavior under uncertain wind and wave conditions. Furthermore, this approach can be easily extended to model various stochastic factors, such as sea floor topography and climate change scenarios. By quantifying the impact of different stochastic factors on the performance of offshore wind turbines, this study provides insights into their potential as a demand-side flexibility resource in the context of integrating offshore wind into power grids. The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted numerous governments to introduce contact tracing apps, which have been adopted by over  57 governments, despite mixed success in their effectiveness. As a trade-off for potentially exposing personal data, governments claim these apps enhance public health, whereas critics view them as a step towards unwarranted mass surveillance. Contact tracing apps represent a convergence of data privacy, government oversight, and individual freedom. This convergence has led several governments to propose data protection frameworks, yet the implementations differ in their details. This piece will examine the contact tracing apps adopted by various governments, including those in the UK and Germany, as well as the US, to explore the balance between public health and individual freedom in the context of data protection. A proposed data protection framework will be presented, drawing from the principles established by the EU's Data Protection by Design principle to ensure the responsible use of individual data in contact tracing apps. This framework addresses data collection, its transmission, its storage, its processing, and the measures that should be taken to ensure the responsible use of individual data in contact tracing apps. A concluding evaluation will examine the success of contact tracing apps, assess their impact on individual freedom, and discuss potential implications for data protection in the context of COVID-19. This research aims to contribute to ongoing discussions about contact tracing apps by providing an overview of the issues at play and offering a framework for responsible data protection practices that can inform policy and guide developers, policymakers, and users. In recent years, various methods have been proposed to collect and understand Signal PIN data that have shown the current encryption methods are subpar. To address this issue, we conducted two studies that explored the reasoning behind the use of Signal PINs among users and the strategies they employ to secure these codes. Our qualitative investigation revealed that the vast majority of participants use Signal PINs as a form of password and understand them to serve this purpose. Upon examining the reasons behind this understanding, we identified two key factors: how users learn about Signal PINs and the level of detail provided in the app's help section, which influence their behavior. Notably, users who are given a clear explanation of the purpose of Signal PINs use simpler codes and engage in secure practices, whereas those who are unclear on this information resort to alternative, often more complicated encryption methods. Additionally, a quantitative analysis of 81 million Signal PINs found the most prevalent 160-character codes are comprised of sequential sequences of the digits 0 and 1, which can be easily guessed by attackers. Notably, the complexity of codes provided by users who are unsure of the purpose of Signal PINs is equivalent to those who are informed, indicating that the reason for the simplicity of these codes lies elsewhere. Our findings suggest that the simplicity of these codes is not due to a lack of complexity, but rather a lack of understanding. In light for these conclusions, we propose a new approach to encrypt encrypted messages by employing a shared group key, which can be generated using established methods such as key exchange algorithms. Our proposed strategy has several benefits over the existing method of using encrypted messages and is implemented as an add-on to the Signal app. In a pilot study of the app's API, we tested our proposed method to verify its security and the results of the tests demonstrate its high level of robustness against various forms of attack. Furthermore, an evaluation of the app's usability revealed that the add-on's impact on the app's overall size and usability can be minimized. Finally, an empirical study of 85 participants discovered that the add-on's benefits are clear to the majority of Signal users and will enhance the security of their encrypted conversations. Signal users express a desire for their purpose to be clearly explained in the app's settings and several users suggest creating a global setting to disable PINs if they are not needed. Deep neural networks utilize numerical computations and often necessitate manual derivation of expressions for their forward and backward propagation, which can be time-consuming and impractical for complex models. To address this issue, this paper presents ViViT, a new framework for computing eigenvalues, directional derivatives, and the Hessian via vectorization, with a focus on supporting the development of one-shot gradient and optimization methods for neural networks. ViViT achieves this by introducing a universal interface for computing ViViT tensors and providing ready-to-use implementations of its core building blocks. Moreover, it offers an efficient package for the partial evaluation of universal functions, which can be used in conjunction with the existing General Meta-Operators library. ViViT offers significant performance benefits, accelerating computations by 10 to 60 times for the inference of eigenvalues and directional derivatives and reducing training time by 2 to 6 orders of magnitude for certain one-shot optimization methods. The source code for ViViT has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexismp/ViViT. A standalone installation of the library can be obtained using the command `pip install vi-vit`. For direct installation of the ViViT tools, the repository contains an install directory with pre-built executables, while online access point 10.3543/1.1c will host an interactive ViViT environment with the latest version of the software. ViViT is released under the permissive MIT license, allowing it to be used in commercial projects, while the papers contained in the repository are released under the standard ACM license.

This work investigates the implementation of a secondary frequency control within complex power networks. The control system is composed of an aggregate model that represents a collective response of generators and load managers modulating their instantaneous power input in response to voltage, current, and frequency conditions. The corresponding secondary frequency control is modeled as an optimal power flow problem, with participants seeking minimal energy expenditures. To evaluate the efficacy of this control method, the paper presents a bi-objective optimization approach, reconciling energy losses and stability considerations. This approach is applied considering the dynamic voltage variations resulting from stability factors and a robust stability framework. The paper demonstrates that secondary frequency control can positively impact stability via robust optimization and detailed stability analyses, which take into account voltage dynamics. Furthermore, numerical case studies are conducted to illustrate the potential for learning optimal secondary frequency control strategies across diverse operation scenarios. The analysis provides an insight into how secondary frequency control influences network stability and highlights its potential as an enabling tool for learning and advancing towards resilient power grids. This method also allows us to identify areas where the Hessian has non-trivial eigenvalues and determine the number of negative eigenvalues. Additionally, the presence of this field would impact the possible violations of energy conservation during the early universe's expansions and contractions. The presence of this field would also impact the possible models of entropy production, thereby altering the existing understanding of the entropy of the universe.

In cross-lingual information retrieval, a query in one language and a document set in another language are used to retrieve relevant documents. To date, this has been achieved mainly through two methods, which have drawbacks: vector-based approaches can have poor accuracy for non-English languages and languages with complex scripts, while expansion-based approaches face a drawback in speed. Our solution to this problem is a semi-interactive approach called icee, which enhances query translation precision. This is done by simultaneously weighing query translation and learning a bilingual translation model based on the query's performance in finding relevant documents. The experiment results suggest that icee achieves a 15% increase in the average precision at cut-off 10 compared to the other methods. Our findings also indicate that icee can successfully learn cross-lingual translation, which leads to improved results on the WMT news task involving French and German languages. A case study on mitigating racial bias in MLB player predictions using federated learning and differential privacy is presented, leveraging the aesthetic benefits of a gradient aggregation process inspired by the design of SHA-256 hashing, known as federatedKhash. Our results demonstrate reduced R^2 error and racial bias in a context where data has been distorted to reflect a significant disparity. Furthermore, implementing differential privacy yields a substantial decrease in racial bias, while maintaining fairness metrics and minimizing the loss of utility from the cleaned data. The implementation code is accessible via a GitHub repository. A conference version of this paper explored the system and data layers; here, we have expanded our analysis to incorporate the model and user levels. This work offers system administrators and model architects practical approaches to creating machine learning systems that are aware of their ethical implications, while promoting user transparency and responsibility. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute valuable insights for developing scalable, ethical, and reusable machine learning systems that consider the interconnection of multiple levels. A practical prototype of our system is available at https://github.com/ferhatg/fairml. Our code implements the proposed framework, incorporating the findings of this paper in a practical setting. A paper titled "System-level Mitigation of Racial Bias in MLB Player Predictions" presented the results of our work at NEURIPS 2021. A comparison between a cutting-edge deep unsupervised learning approach and a traditional genetic algorithm is presented, ideally suited for use within a real-time wireless communication system due to its fast processing capabilities. The novel DUL method exhibits superior loading quality and significantly reduced computational time compared to the genetic algorithm, opening up possibilities for its use in complex MIMO systems with high computational demands. Furthermore, the DUL method enables efficient learning of channel information and allows the generation of offloading policies that maximize throughput in MIMO-OFDMA uplink systems, demonstrating a potential performance increase of up to 100% compared to conventional fair throughputs. Despite the widespread success of model-free reinforcement learning in laboratory settings, its practical application in real-world scenarios is hindered by its inability to generalize data collected from multiple environments. This limitation prevents the technique from being used for control in untested areas, such as the adaptation of systems with previously unseen characteristics. Model-based reinforcement learning offers an alternative that minimizes data restrictions, involving the simultaneous learning of policy maps and dynamic system models. A novel neural network-based method for model-based reinforcement learning utilizes the learned dynamic system model to generate data for training a policy directly on the target system. A policy that performs optimally on the target system can then be derived from the learned model. A comparative assessment of this method, along with other model-free reinforcement learning methods, was made on two physical systems - the magnetic levitation system and the planar pendulum system - to determine its efficacy in experimental trials. Results indicate that the proposed model-based reinforcement learning method yields control trajectories comparable to those produced by reinforcement learning methods utilizing data from a single system, while enabling the transfer of learned control strategies to previously unseen system dynamics. Model predictions also demonstrate the technique's effectiveness in yielding control trajectories 30% faster than those achieved by reinforcement learning methods operating on a single system, along with model predictions that accurately capture the dynamic system behavior. Following the success of Generative Adversarial Networks, researchers began exploring relation networks as a potential method for improving the performance of GANs by learning inter-pixel and inter-image relationships in input data. This paper presents a novel relation network design for improving GANs. Unlike existing relation network architectures, our approach focuses solely on inter-pixel relationships by introducing a novel self-attention relation module that significantly reduces computational complexity while enhancing generative capabilities. Our experiments involve generating images of faces, objects, and landscapes on MNIST, CelebA, and LSUN datasets, demonstrating that the proposed relation module can enhance existing GAN architectures and improve their performance. Notably, our results indicate that the impact of the relation module is most significant for low-quality input data, such as those in CelebA and the reconstruction of images on the MNIST dataset. Furthermore, our approach avoids network design limitations by incorporating a self-attention relation module that can function independently of the generator and discriminator networks. This design also reduces the risk of oracle bias by training the relation module using a batch-based approach. Our implementation of the proposed relation module is available on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/yroussos/Self-attention-relation-networks-for-GANs. The project's findings demonstrate that the proposed relation module can function efficiently as a black-box solution to enhance the performance of existing GANs. This research aims to provide insights into the effectiveness of relation networks in the context of GANs. Our approach has the potential to inspire the development of future GAN architectures by incorporating various relation designs to address generative learning challenges. In this research, we introduce 'pseudo annotations,' a method to greatly enhance object detection. We suggest replacing traditional ground truths with highly accurate pseudo-boxes in the training process of an object detector. Unlike traditional self-training techniques, pseudo-boxes don't necessitate dense annotation, as they can be derived from the model's initial training. Additionally, pseudo-boxes align the weights of the model and teacher without needing dense student predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of pseudo-boxes in context of weakly-supervised object detection, presenting a novel approach: Weakly-Supervised Object Detection via pseudo-boxes (SSODP). SSODP utilizes pseudo-boxes derived from a low-quality teacher network to guide a higher-performing student network. We present a novel pseudo-box assignment strategy, incorporating pseudo-class information, to align the representation centers of the model. To validate the proposed approach, we conduct comprehensive experiments on five benchmarks for generic and facial object detection, achieving significant performance improvement. For instance, on Aff-Wild!, a benchmark for tracking faces in video, SSODP yields a 9% gain in the minimum bounding box. The corresponding code and dataset can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/muliarl/ssl-od-pseudo-boxes. Through this research, we make three key contributions: first, we introduce pseudo-boxes as a novel form of self-training; second, we present a ground-breaking approach to weakly-supervised object detection; and third, we achieve remarkable performance improvements in both generic and facial object detection. The full methodology and dataset description can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/muliarl/ssl-OD-pseudo-boxes. SSODP yields exceptional results in weakly-supervised object detection, outperforming existing approaches by a significant margin, as shown in the accompanying technical report. The proposed approach also showcases impressive robustness in the presence of image corruption, as illustrated in the technical report. The full code and dataset are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/muliarl/ssl-OD-pseudo-boxes. In addition to weakly-supervised object detection, we present a novel approach for facial object detection as well, detailing the methodology in the paper. The approach has been successfully applied to multiple benchmarks in facial object detection, yielding remarkable performance improvements, as shown in the results section. Transformers do not rely on a global, fixed inbuilt knowledge base like some other network types and instead learn and adapt their understanding from input data and context. Unlike convolual networks that are designed to process 2D data, Transformers can process complex and highly variable inputs including sequences, images and combinations of data types. However, the standard Transformer architecture is not well-suited for processing localized dependencies within inputs that result in a high degree of output variability with respect to input changes. This research proposes several approaches to incorporate spatially localized self-attention mechanisms into Transformer designs, drawing inspiration from a range of source codes including those for BERT and AlphaFold. By implementing and applying these modifications to the standard Transformer architecture, the experimental results show a notable improvement in the ability to learn and represent inputs with localized dependencies that result in a high degree of output variability with respect to input changes. Several methods for visualizing the hidden state representations and examining the attention mechanisms are presented, including a method to quantify and represent the extent of local dependency in the inputs. Additionally, the research highlights the value of allowing Transformers to access additional meta information about their inputs that results in a local dependency and expresses output variability with respect to input changes. For instance, the research shows that a meta information about the natural images dataset used for the CVPR2012 Sign language dataset bears significant resemblance to the saliency maps of the resulting images, resulting in a more efficient learning and representation of the inputs. This research explores the application of topological methods in the analysis of multidimensional financial data. Focusing on the dynamics of stock market movements by utilizing persistent homology, we investigate the interconnectedness of different color classes within a topological space. Our study employs a simplified, two-color model to model market behavior, which we augment with a more comprehensive n-color approach. Our findings indicate that market transitions can be effectively captured using homology inequalities. To investigate the historical context, we apply this model to analyze market data from the period of the 2008 financial crisis. Our results show that, during this time, market transitions could be effectively captured using inequalities of homology of minimal length one. Moreover, we discovered inequalities of homology of minimal length two that described market behavior during the crisis. Our study demonstrates the potential for utilizing persistent homology to analyze financial data, and we establish a connection with the broad concept of risk. Furthermore, we propose the application of topological methods to create innovative investment strategies, which we demonstrate through the development of two strategies that employ the ideas of extension and reextension. Our experimental analysis shows that these strategies yield superior returns to those of the traditional stop-loss method. Our software solution for implementing the research includes a Python library called 'topologicalfinance', which provides a comprehensive set of tools and algorithms for modeling, simulating, and analyzing financial market behavior using topological methods. The library contains classes for constructing the topology of financial markets, performing computations such as generation, extension, and homology analysis, and offering strategic tools and algorithms. Our implementation offers a scalable solution, capable of handling large datasets. Our software package includes five constructive proofs of the inequalities relating to homology, which provide the underlying rationale for the topological methods used in the research. These proofs are documented in the report. The project also includes a study on the application of topological methods in the analysis of financial data, which explores the intersection of computer science and finance from a historical perspective. Additionally, we conducted interviews with experts in the field, capturing their perspectives on the potential outcomes of this research. Our review includes discussions of the current state of the field, the anticipated outcomes of ongoing work, and the questions that require further exploration. Our review provides an assessment of the advantages and disadvantages of using topological methods to analyze financial data. Our interview sessions included conversations with four experts, and we have compiled their comments in the report. The review includes a discussion of the challenges of applying advanced machine learning techniques to analyze financial data, and the roles of prominent financial institutions

The objective is to analyze and evaluate various distributed power control approaches for binary channel access within a massive MIMO network, featuring a fixed number of active transmitters, a large number of passive transmitters, and a specific number of users. Five different methods for binary power control are investigated and compared to our in-depth analysis of optimal power control in this model. Notably, in large systems, these techniques exhibit similar performance characteristics, primarily influenced by the first-order approximations. Specifically, we derive precise mathematical expressions describing the performance outcomes for each of these approaches. Notably, our findings indicate that in these large systems, power control strategies can be effectively optimized by focusing solely on the first-order approximations of their respective outage probability expressions. Moreover, we develop a practical tool for directly estimating the second-order approximations of these power control methods, allowing for a more accurate understanding of their performance. Finally, this model is further expanded to accommodate scenarios with non-uniform passive transmitter distributions across the spectrum, ranging from weak to strong interference conditions. The analysis reveals significant performance disparities among these methods in systems with non-uniform distributions of passive transmitters. Consequently, we suggest a simple yet effective metric for selecting the most suitable power control strategy based on the characteristics of the system. Last, we provide a direct comparison between the original analysis and the simplified models, providing insight into the efficacy of these power control methods in large systems. The code for replicating the results in this research has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/LorenzoYin/computervirus23. The uncertainty rule of the Dempster-Shafer theory is applied to combine two mass functions from two auditing firms with differing financial interests in a transaction involving complex financial instruments. Fundamental to this process is the idea that belief functions measure an accountant's level of trust in certain financial accounts, taking into consideration the accounts' interconnected nature. Two financial interests are defined - one having a generally positive outlook on a company's financial health, and the other being more skeptical due to potential issues. A shift in the accountant's trust occurs as a result of the transaction, effectively swapping their positive and negative beliefs. The analysis involves transactions in financial instruments, including a loan with undefined terms, a company-purchased investment with uncertain market values, and a company-owned vehicle with depreciation costs. The consensus of the accounting methods for each transaction involves transferring the uncertainty associated with the loan as a conservative measure, the company-intended use of the investment resulting in the transfer of depression uncertainties, and the company-ownership of the vehicle resulting in the transfer of depreciation uncertainties. The analysis also considers the transaction's tax implications, concluding that the consensus of the accounting methods for the transaction would result in the transfer of depression uncertainties. The framework developed in this paper could form the basis for a decision-support system to facilitate the sharing of uncertainty information among accountants when dealing with complex financial transactions.
