Methods efficient in simulating spatial point processes while meeting exactness requirements often rely on approximations, though, in most cases, the accuracy of these approximations remains unknown. In contrast, a recently developed technique employs acceptance-rejection principles to create, conditionally on the accepted points, independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) process simulations. This technique opens up a new strategy to simulate Poisson processes: By integrating acceptance-rejection approximations, one can simulate slightly over-dispered Poisson processes with known approximation errors. Building on this, a multi-scale approach allows a dynamic balance between exactness and approximation, this is particularly useful in simulations of high spatially varying Poisson processes. This is a practical guide to implementing the presented methods and will demonstrate their efficiency in realistic applications. Computer code to reproduce the findings in this article is available online. Additionally, a novel approach for simulating generalized Pareto processes--a flexible model for extreme events--is presented. This involves efficiently simulating -monotonically generalized Pareto processes, followed by a Poisson process warping technique to create the generalized Pareto process. Examples of modeling extreme events in the context of spatial statistics are provided. This includes modeling data from extremes in the Earth's atmosphere and modeling tail behavior of rainfall data. Finally, a simulation study evaluates the finite sample properties of estimators based on generalized Pareto process models. Results show that these estimators can benefit from the use of simulated process realizations, allowing for improved confidence intervals in modeling extreme events. All the presented methods have been implemented in a R package named spatstats, which includes additional relevant functionality. Further details on the novel simulation methods can be found in a supplementary paper, where these methods are extended to include simulations of multivariate and clustered point processes. Generalization to n-dimensional space is also possible. This research forms the basis of a PhD thesis, which explores the theoretical implications of the presented methods. In the PhD, the practical strategy to simulate Poisson processes is idealized, and the parameters involved are treated as random variables. This is a supplementary paper to an earlier article, where the acceptance-rejection strategy is initially presented. Building on the concepts in this article, a new algorithm for simulating spatial random fields is introduced in a further paper, which generalizes the approach to any random field. These methods are now freely available in an R package called spatcluster, which includes additional functionality. A companion to this article can be found in a paper, where the simulated models are used to estimate the tail behavior of rainfall

In a multitasking environment, varying the allocation of processing capacity among tasks is known as "coarse-grained" or "dynamic" scheduling. This study investigates how adjusting the distribution of task processing capacity affects time and scheduling policies. Analyzing a system with constantly arriving and finishing tasks, we found that the way they interact with each other and with sharing coefficients significantly impacts performance. Based on theoretical production models, we developed eight general scenarios representing different task relationships. In two of these scenarios, we determined closed-form expressions for system performance, while in the other six scenarios this expression cannot be closed. To address these situations, we used approximation theory, leading to generic and generic approximations. Our findings show that when tasks are independent, a simple ratio expression closely estimates the system's performance. By combining the generic approximations, we developed the approximate production models representing complex systems, which exhibit moderate error rates. These models enable performance evaluation and allow for the assessment of processing capacity sharing on the system's performance. Moreover, they enable the derivation of time scheduling policies that maintain a balanced mean response time and mean work load in the system. These policies can be used directly in systems with few tasks or as a starting point for more complex systems where a precise method for performance evaluation is not available. Our experimental study revealed that a simple look-up method in a table effectively estimates the error in scenarios with low or medium error rates and allows for comparable response times to those achieved by exact methods. This look-up method can be applied in practice and its implementation is straightforward. Our experimental study further showed that when the ratio of task sharing varies, the performance levels of the system change significantly. Our analysis and experimental findings suggest the following generic properties of the system: (i) increasing the ratio of task sharing and the dependency between tasks A and B decreases the error rate and the response time; (ii) an inverse relationship exists between the ratio of task sharing and the error rate and the response time; (iii) an equal sharing of task processing capacity minimizes the error rate and the response time; (iv) the error rate and the response time of tasks A and B are influenced differently based on their relationship, where in most cases an approximate factor greater than one is observed. These implications indicate that changing the ratio of task sharing in a multitasking environment impacts system performance and scheduling policies. Our findings can guide practitioners in determining appropriate sharing ratios and time scheduling policies to maintain optimal performance in such systems. IoT device management, particularly firmware updates, has evolved into a complex task due to the rapid expansion of large-scale IoT deployments. Given the dimensions of such deployments, scalability and reliability are crucial considerations. We propose a framework called Kaidos for efficiently updating large numbers of IoT devices simultaneously, without relying on central infrastructure and using cryptographic methods to ensure integrity and validity. Furthermore, to minimize the impact of critical updates on device performance, two concurrent updating strategies have been developed. These strategies aim to reduce updates to a manageable size for individual devices and reduce the load on devices during the process. We tested and validated the performance of Kaidos using 105, 122, and 158 wireless sensor nodes. The results demonstrate its capability to update large numbers of IoT devices rapidly, securely, and reliably, with a high success rate of 99.98\% or higher. The concurrent strategies developed proved to outperform sequential updating methods, reducing the time required to update a single device by 71\% on average. Consequently, the proposed Kaidos system boasts a remarkable update speed of up to 512 times faster than updating each device individually. The adoption of Kaidos can yield substantial cost savings, saving as much as 84\% to 95\% of the bandwidth needed for updates compared to other methods. A comprehensive security analysis of the system was conducted, showing that it encounters a limited number of attack attempts while updating 122 IoT devices in a wireless network. The results demonstrate a successful attack resistance rate of 99.985% and an attack attempt-to-successful-attack ratio of 0.000415%. This research proves the scalability and reliability of the proposed system, making it suitable for updating IoT devices in the most diverse applications. To facilitate reproducibility, the entire source code of the Kaidos framework, along with the test software, is available for open use at the repository https://github.com/ulldk/kaidos. All the experimental data have been uploaded to the repository as well. Moreover, to ensure the system's validity, the test results have been uploaded to the repository in the form of a PowerPoint file. Furthermore, a tool called update-generator, which supports the Kaidos framework, is available for open use at the repository https://github.com/ulldk/generatore-updates. All the experimental data have been uploaded to the repository in the form of a PowerShell script. Moreover, a detailed description of the proposal has been uploaded to the repository in the form of a PDF file

These results, obtained using a level statistics based approach, are independent of time and scale. To further understand this phenomenon, scientists used a model to recreate the system's Hamiltonian and examined its behavior. They discovered that in the early stages of the transition, the system undergoes a process where it jumps between states with high and low entropy. The model revealed that these fluctuations can be explained by a resonance phenomenon. When two partial entropies are close, a characteristic fractal region forms, resulting in a high fractal dimension of the self-energy. In this research, scientists have explained how this phenomenon occurs and have found additional indications of phase space volume collapse during the transition. Their findings confirm that eigenstate entropy is an accurate indicator of this process. However, they also discovered that in the late stages of the transition, this indicator becomes less reliable. To provide a clearer understanding of this process, scientists have created a diagram illustrating the phase space of a system in the early and late stages of the transition. A recently introduced kBM-DP+ algorithm enhances the capacity of dynamic programming to solve the MultipleTargets problem efficiently within k steps, while also minimizing computational time and memory usage. By approximating target probability distributions with a smaller, fixed size multi-Gaussian mixture, the algorithm achieves a significant reduction in computational complexity compared to previous models, such as the influential Block-Junction Tree (BJT) model. In fact, the kBM-DP+ algorithm demonstrates nearly linear time and logarithmic space complexity, making it a scalable solution for probabilistic inference in large networks with numerous random variables. Furthermore, the BJTDiverge algorithm is also presented to assess the distance between probability distributions represented by BJT and kBM-DP+, providing a metric to evaluate approximation quality and design choices. Extensive empirical evaluations showcase the BJTDiverge algorithm's practical utility in data-driven modeling, where it helps refine probabilistic models by identifying variables to improve the current model's fit to data. Overall, the kBM-DP+ algorithm offers a valuable tool for inference in discrete probabilistic networks with an adaptable complexity trade-off, making it a suitable replacement for the BJT model in various applications. The software implementing these algorithms is freely available at https://github.com/Jesus-Villella/bjt-diverge. Moreover, a CPLEX-based extension of the kBM-DP+ algorithm is provided to solve the Generalized Maximal Perfect Matchings problem, which finds extensive applications in computer science. In this context, the algorithm exhibits a polyhedron extension property and a novel technique is proposed to efficiently utilize precomputed elements of the general perfect matching polyhedron to accelerate the algorithm. The polyhedral extension technique shows promise in reducing computational complexity by avoiding the need to repeatedly solve the Generalized Maximal Perfect Matchings problem from scratch. Instead, the method leverages previously computed GMP vertices and cuts to accelerate kBM-DP+ algorithm performance, especially when dealing with scenarios where the parameter k is relatively small. The proposed technique achieves sublinear time complexity benefits in practice. Validating the accuracy of a system's responses is a crucial component that enhances the capabilities and reliability of a technical system, particularly one employed by a human operator. In the context of temporal planning, we have developed a validation algorithm that identifies system responses as valid or invalid, which can be done concurrently with the generation of options. We discovered that this validation algorithm has the potential to decrease the time it takes for the system to produce options and make them available for selection, as well as reduce the operator's task burden. Specifically, the study showed a median of 62% reduction in the time to display options and a 45% reduction in task burden when the algorithm was used. Notably, in approximately 18% of cases, the algorithm was able to begin generating options sooner than the original system, demonstrating a notable improvement. Overall, our research indicates that the value of a temporal planning system can be increased through the incorporation of validation algorithms that increase its speed and reliability. Moreover, we have identified areas where future developments can incorporate validation mechanisms to further amplify the impact of such systems on task burden and information quality. As a practical consequence, we have made available a version of the LAMA planner that incorporates this validation algorithm, with the goal of supporting the development of human operator models. We believe that this algorithm has the potential to benefit other planning-based systems used in conjunction with human operators. Moreover, we have identified opportunities for future research to further reduce the time it takes for human operators to use these systems, making them more effective and increasing their usefulness. learning techniques. Overall, the study makes a practical contribution by
catapulting this class of research into real-world contexts, while also

These data streams frequently contain missing values that need to be addressed, making both stream processing and knowledge graph construction challenging tasks that require efficient handling of velocity and voluminous data with possible value obsolescence. Existing stream-based graph construction methods fail to prioritize data velocity, manage voluminous data effectively, or consider value obsolescence, making them less suitable for future IoT data applications. 

To address these limitations, we introduce H-STREAM, a novel stream processing framework specifically designed for constructing large-scale knowledge graphs from IoT data streams. H-STREAM boasts advanced capabilities to handle violent data velocities, massive data volumes with limitless storage, and dynamic value maintenance through a modular and efficient processing system, all while accommodating evolving data streams. This framework comprises (1) a modular processing module that handles data generation, transformation, and graph construction across scalable microservices, scalable microservices across multiple containers; (2) a module for parallel data processing via a Map-Reduce algorithm; (3) a module for synchronizing data, ensuring data consistency, and dynamically adding or removing nodes as needed; (4) a module for supporting value obsolescence using a Lambda-tuple labeling method; (3) a module for storing data using GraphDB, providing additional functionality for managing large-scale graphs. 

H-STREAM offers a new approach for constructing large-scale knowledge graphs from IoT data streams with evolving values, offering unprecedented performance and scalability capabilities for handling massive data streams with unlimited storage capabilities, making it an ideal solution for data stream velocity and volume challenges. 

We tested H-STREAM on single-node and cluster platforms with impressive results across a range of metrics, demonstrating its superior performance and scalability when building knowledge graphs from IoT data using common knowledge graph construction algorithms, showing a significant improvement in processing time and efficiency compared to industry standards, offering an ideal solution for data integration and mediation across IoT applications, particularly those utilizing data stream technologies to construct large-scale knowledge graphs with evolving values. 

We believe H-STREAM, a novel stream-based graph construction method, offers a complete and efficient solution for constructing large-scale knowledge graphs from IoT data streams with unlimited velocity, volume, and obsolescence capabilities, making it an ideal choice for data integration and mediation on large-scale IoT platforms, particularly those utilizing data stream technologies.

To this end, we're exploring the use of paper metadata and authorship information as a studying tool. Our approach involves examining publishing venues and authors to track field development, and we've specifically looked at the relationship between DBLP entries, focusing on the changes in their categorization and the venues at which they were published over time. Our methodology is akin to topic modeling, utilizing an unsupervised word embedding analysis with sanctions to map authorship and venues into a stable framework. Our results offer insights into both the growth of Computer Science fields and the shifts in their boundaries, and we observe that some categories have made significant progress in becoming established as distinct areas of study. Our analysis also reveals the impact of influential conferences and the shifts in their hierarchies, and we find that the field of computer learning has expanded to encompass a broader understanding of itself. Our data is available online, and we're exploring its potential applications in studying academic openness, as well as the changes in text content over time. Additionally, we're developing a semantically enriched version of DBLP, enriched with concepts drawn from Wikidata and WordNet, and we're studying the position of DBLP entries using the HeteroKnowledgeGraph, a larger knowledge base that incorporates DBLP, Wikidata, and WordNet. We introduce a novel method to resolve two primary flaws in traditional clustering approaches, particularly evident in the single-linkage clustering algorithm. These shortcomings lead to 'clusterings' that cannot be regarded as inherent cluster structures. To address this issue, we developed a framework that leverages categorical properties and minimizes the likelihood of'spurious' cluster structures appearing in the resulting functorial clustering schemes. In doing so, this method ensures that any cluster scheme derived from a funtorial scheme, including single-linkage, will lack the'spurious' issue. Specifically, this approach works by establishing a cluster scheme based on a level set of the clustering functor rather than its domain. Functorial schemes are shown to possess'stability': a cluster scheme derived from one object often matches the one obtained with a slightly altered version of the clustering functor. Slightly altered here means a version of the clustering functor that only introduces additional clusters from some limited pool. A clustering version of Ershov functors, which concerns the computation of finite varieties in the simple model $T_0$, is also developed. This research investigates the real-time completion of video data by considering a significant aspect: video frame movement. We introduce STC-MV, the first streaming algorithm designed to tackle this challenge. It complements existing streaming tensor completion methods with a new model of motion vectors, thereby extending the Cottermoreau method to a tensor of order three. We perform comprehensive experiments to evaluate the proposed approach. We demonstrate that standard methods fail when dealing with video data due to changing frame orientations. In contrast, STC-MV delivers superior results with substantial improvements in PSNR and SSIM, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency on various video datasets. The code for this research is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ NguyenBaDung/STC_MV. Additionally, the proposed method has been submitted for publication due to space limitations in this work. We anticipate STC-MV to contribute positively to the field. A common pattern is identified in random walks and page ranking algorithms, as well as in more complex models such as learned optimal policies, where a graph is repeatedly normalized to remove self-loops and the corresponding probability distributions converge. The iterative graph normalization process is explored in the context of its natural higher-dimensional extension, where a flow is optimized to remove self-loops. This iteration is shown to correspond to a specific type of iterative algorithm called a Newton iteration, which is usually applied to a function whose key property is that taking its derivative twice leads to a function whose maximum value is at most one. The study of this iterated Newton method, along with other related concepts, such as quadratic systems, and their connection to unique solutions, sheds new light on the process of iterative graph normalization. The conclusion involves the complex nature of the iterated Newton method, and its potential implications for understanding the complex dynamics often observed in optimal policy learning problems. The potential for improving the speed of convergence of iterative graph normalization is discussed, and specifically, the case of learned optimal policies, where a connection to unique solutions is made via the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem, and an approximate algorithm for this problem with a $O(\log N)$ approximation factor is proposed, along with a corresponding $O(1/\log N)$ convergence rate for the iterated Newton method. The M dwarf binary system CR Dra consists of two closely tied together stars that create a dense disk and produce powerful magnetic fields. The system's activity level currently sits in a moderate state, which has allowed scientists to observe a radio emissions emanating from the pair through regular checks. It has been found that CR Dra's activity levels periodically fluctuate over approximately 3.8 years, which has prompted scientists to place current radio emissions estimates as of mid-2020. Data collected by the Very Large Array in 2020 showed CR Dra's radio emissions taking the form of circularly polarized plumes extending towards the outside; the observed type III interplanetary emissions shared the same direction as the stars' rotation. Further research has also indicated that ANR can efficiently be applied to other areas such as creating video editing software of the future. Artificial neural networks excel at recognizing images, but humans struggle with severely distorted images. To better comprehend humans' visual capabilities, it is necessary to develop tests that challenge their visual intuition. For this purpose, a distorted version of the widely-used ImageNet dataset was created, employing multiple methods of distortion. The new dataset, dubbed NetNet, enables accurate comparison between human and machine visual processing. The NetNet dataset showcases distortions that are imperceptible to humans but pose a problem for state-of-the-art neural networks. The new dataset is employed in two experiments to assess humans' visual tolerance. The outcomes indicate that humans' visual limits align more closely with those of a strong neural network model than a weak one. Moreover, by analyzing humans' mistakes on the NetNet dataset, it is suggested that there is a link between human errors and similarities between images represented in a specific space. The NetNet dataset and associated code are publicly available at netnet.dataset (https://sgruder.dev/NetNet). The NetNet dataset contains images distorted using various algorithms such as Gaussian noise, removal of colors, binary conversion, removal of parts, and a novel method called WordSwap that replaces local image patches with random words. When viewed by humans as visual noise, these images are also hard for state-of-the-art neural networks to classify. In a direct comparison with Imagenet-L, NetNet reveals that some distortions that are imperceptible to humans have a smaller impact on neural networks classification errors. In two controlled studies, humans' visual limits were found to coincide more closely with those of a strong neural network model than a weak one. In an alternative evaluation, humans' mistakes on the NetNet dataset were found to share similarities with similarities between images represented in a specific space. These findings support the idea that humans' visual errors and neural networks' mistakes share a shared underlying mechanism. These conclusions are further validated when considered in the context of visual anomalies, humans' visual limitations in other contexts, and other datasets such as COCO, VGG Fish, VGG Wildlife and Google QuickDraw. We are evaluating Wilson loops in Chern-Simons theory, specifically with various twists, to demonstrate that their associated matrices follow patterns established by the Askey-Wilson algebra. In the case of the exotic Wilson loop, the resulting matrices generate the AW algebra directly, whereas matrices derived from the normal Wilson loop undergo additional transformations, specifically Wilson Wilson generators, that are also part of the AW algebra. Our discussion will be expanded to include Wilson loops in higher-dimensional Chern-Simons theories, where these similarly relate to the generators of the double Askey-Wilson algebra. These findings are a key component of larger constructions that use Wilson loops to create elements of the AW and DAW algebra. Furthermore, the relationships we've discovered offer new insights into the broader theory of Chern-Simons observables. The underlying mathematics involves a combination of Wilson loops, three-geometries, and the Reidemeister move relation, all components of a more comprehensive framework for quantum geometry. In support of this claim, we'll examine how Chern-Simons theory in three dimensions resolves a specific problem from the 1980s that relates to the algebraic properties of the AW. In addition, the discussion will explore connections between the exponential form of the Wilson loop and two other important objects: the responsible matrix, which can be constructed from the BMS three-algebra, and the Dunkl Wilson loop. This relationship is particularly notable because the responsible matrix, which generates the DW algebra, has implications for symmetry and the breaking of scale invariance. In relation to the breaking of scale, which has been a focus of recent research in the field, we'll show that the AW and DAW algebra can be reinterpreted as the invariant subalgebra of the BMS three-algebra under a specific symmetry transformation. This symmetry transformation is similar to one proposed by Hořava in 2009 in an attempt to revive scale symmetry. Despite this connection, the discussion will reveal an important difference between our interpretation of the DW algebra and scale symmetry. Instead, the discussion will reveal an analogy between the DW algebra and the finite diffeomorphism symmetry. In the process of these derivations, we'll analyze Wilson loops in higher-dimensional Chern-Simons theories, which have previously unexplored properties, and show that, contrary to expectations, these loops do not exhibit duality. This result stems from a key insight into Chern-Simons theories in higher dimensions, which have both Wilson loops with a dual counterpart, denoted as exotic, and those without, normal.

Our study focuses on how the representation of a fermi sea in a three-part quantum system affects the likelihood weights used in quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The research shows that utilizing a trimer-based computational basis at low temperatures results in serious issues with weightings, as they fail to connect with the known fermi sea ground state. In order to minimize these errors, we modified the basis to always include at least one unpaired particle, even in a trimerized configuration, by forcing one particle to leave the closed shell. This research explores the application of neural observers to determine the current state of complex systems, using a nonlinear model of disease spread, and evaluates the effectiveness of novel observer designs in contrast to traditional approaches. Six distinct observer strategies are presented, each tailored to the model's nonlinear nature, and their performance is assessed in terms of both the precision of state estimates and the efficacy of their corresponding estimators. Simulation studies of a particular epidemic model reveal that the proposed observers achieve more accurate state estimates and generate more meaningful estimates of infection histories compared to a classic observer, with resulting estimates spanning a narrower interval and exhibiting reduced variability. Furthermore, the research highlights the dependence of observer precision on the choice of estimation horizon and the level of uncertainty associated with model parameters. Crucially, the results indicate the potential for applications of neural observers in analyzing intricate systems beyond the epidemic model, as hinted at through a brief consideration of the application of neural observers to crowds and olfactory spread. Future work could involve extending the findings to scenarios involving stochastic disease models and uncovering the conditions under which the proposed observers yield precise state estimates. Additionally, the research suggests the potential for neural observers to produce more accurate forecasts of system dynamics compared to classical approaches, a possibility that merits explicit exploration in future work. Finally, the results raise important ethical considerations, as the accuracy of neural observers in recovering infection histories raises questions about the invasiveness of these complex tools, a topic that requires further exploration. As part of this research, the code and data for the study have been made publicly available for the scientific community to access and reproduce the results. In the context of asynchronous online federated learning, where nodes don't know the structure of the aggregated model, we explore how to optimize communication for clients. By realizing that the gradient computation doesn't depend on previous rounds' computations, we can reduce the communication overhead. In the standard framework, the parameter update process necessarily depends on past rounds' parameters, resulting in unnecessary computation and extra communication. We introduce a partial-sharing mechanism to mitigate this issue. By sharing the dependent components of the gradient computation instead of the entire model, we can significantly reduce the communication overhead. Moreover, by observing that the gradient computation necessarily doesn't use outdated parameters, we can further optimize communication and eliminate unnecessary transmissions. The proposed methods have been experimentally validated and have the potential to enhance scalability in real-world applications. The partial-sharing mechanism is compatible with existing optimization algorithms and flexible shared parameters can be easily integrated into current frameworks. We also released an open-source library for asynchronous online federated learning to facilitate future optimizations. The proposed methods are accessible through the updated FEDERATE library. In particular, the library now includes an implementation of the partial-sharing mechanism to facilitate widespread evaluation and experimentation. We seek to establish a unified benchmark platform for online federated learning. The updated library and associated codes are available at https://github.com/uefaas/FEDERATE. To address this challenge, this research first establishes exact expressions for real and imaginary parts of large exponential map powers, providing highly accurate approximations with a simplified error term. In addition to these findings, closed-form formulas are derived for real and imaginary parts of large composite exponential map powers, with further constant factor multipliers. These formulas are attributed to previously unknown real and imaginary part expressions of complex Chebyshev polynomials. Consequently, this research develops new efficient methods for approximating the numerical range of the exponential map near critical points and the self-intersections of its iterated versions. It also translates existing real Chebyshev polynomial expressions into complex forms, while also discovering new connections between the ranges of the exponential map and complex Fibonacci polynomials. Furthermore, this research provides a new representation of the real variable binary Gaussian hypergeometric function in terms of the real part of the complex variable hypergeometric function, highlighting its potential applications in the field of computer graphics by facilitating the smooth shading of complex shapes in 3D clipping. In the last few years, the use of pressurized tobacco products has been linked to growing health and respiratory concerns. Our research focuses on understanding the workings of these devices through computational modeling and simulation. 

Previous studies and experiments revealed that the unique two-chamber design of these devices contributes to higher vapor density during the puffing process. This paper explores the effect of the two-chamber design on gas expansion and contraction when no pressure is applied. 

We conducted experiments and simulations to compare the characteristics of single and two-chamber devices made from different materials. The results showed that the two-chamber design reduces the rate of pressure drop in air-filled chambers. 

However, the two-chamber design has little impact on the rate of vaporization. We suggest that optimizing the two-chamber design, combined with minimizing vaporization area, could significantly improve the efficiency of vaporization. 

Our study lays the groundwork for further investigations into the two-chamber design of pressurized tobacco products. 

The principles discovered may also be applicable to other types of devices that utilize a similar vaporization mechanism found in certain e-cigarette designs. 

Our computational models provide a detailed simulation of pressurized tobacco products, from chamber volume to sub-micron gas bubble formation. 

Our studies reveal the complex interactions within pressurized tobacco products, involving fluid dynamics, heat transfer, and non-conditional mixing. 

Evaluating existing pressurized tobacco product technologies against their competitors - original tobacco, e-cigarettes, and advanced aerosol devices - helps us identify their strengths and weaknesses and assess their potential threat to public health in terms of their performance and operation principles. 

Ultimately, fundamental insights into the interaction of heat, mass, and momentum transfer can inform the development of better devices for both conventional and alternative smoking devices. 

The primary data released as part of this research includes various pressurized tobacco product designs, aerosol dynamics, and generalized modeling parameters for different smoking devices. 

The employed computational framework was validated against and in conjunction with several pressurized tobacco product data, e-cigarette technology, and advanced lung device information.

The success of recommendation systems largely relies on the user's experience, and understanding their intent is paramount for optimizing those systems. Unlike general intent recognition tasks that can utilize static knowledge, intent-based recommendation tasks require dynamic user interactions to infer intent. Past approaches to model intent-based recommendations have been largely confined to simple scenarios, and there's a lack of research on more complex models that can handle large-scale and real-time recommendation requirements. This paper proposes a scalable model for complex user intent learning in large-scale recommendation systems, and we showcase this model's efficacy on a massive video recommendation platform with over 500 million daily users. Our model reduces the number of requirements computations by 50% and has minimal additional computational overhead. We also found that providing an intent mask can boost a next item recommendation model's AUC by 2.1% and MRR by 6.6% compared to a baseline model. This research is currently in production on a major online video platform with over 50 million daily viewers. We are proud of the substantial improvements to user engagement metrics we've achieved, including a 58% increase in co-clicks and an 8% decrease in deserted carts. We are proud of the substantial improvements to user engagement metrics we've achieved, and plan to apply the lessons we've learned to other recommendation tasks in the future. A key aspect of this setting involves a function $f(\mathbf{M}_i,\mathbf{J})$ that maps matrix $\mathbf{M}_i$ to output $f(\mathbf{M}_i,\mathbf{J})$, utilizing a secret matrix $\mathbf{J}$. The goal of the learner is to deduce the matrix $\mathbf{J}$ from the combined data set $\{f(\mathbf{M}_i,\mathbf{J})\}_{i=1^n}$.

We establish a PCA-type technique that achieves sample complexity $S^{\frac{1}{2}\alpha_2(\mathbf{J})}$, which surpasses the previous best result of $S^{\frac{1}{2}\alpha_2(\mathbf{J})}\log S$. The technique is based on analyzing a weighted combination of the data and utilizing the triangle inequality, while in the process of solving the optimization problem, it can be shown that the solution converges to the original matrix $\mathbf{J}$. We found that the first-order stationary points of our objective function are close to the optimal solution, which has a small gap for specific property conditions and can be made nearly zero under general circumstances.

In response to changing environmental conditions and variations, species populations undergo selective adjustments. The widely accepted premise in ecology that warmer and more mutated species thrive in more energetic environments needs revision because current theoretical models exhibit multiple possible outcomes. We conduct an in-depth examination of several attacks against speech representation learning (SRL) models, with a focus on how effective they are against various types of attackers, ranging from those with no knowledge to specialized attackers (${{\mathcal{A}}_{\mathrm{Z}}}$). We discover that the effectiveness of SRL attacks can be heavily influenced by factors such as the type of attack, the specific SRL module that is targeted, as well as the source of the attack data. In addition to our findings on the vulnerability of SRL models, we propose a new attack technique, called the proxy attack, where the attacker first identifies a model that predicts speech detection with a high level of accuracy, and then utilizes this information to locate the sensitive part of the input audio data. We observe that the proxy attack is particularly successful against models that are trained for speech detection, achieving a high attack success rate of 0.90 when tested on a large dataset. We observe that the effectiveness of other attacks against SRL models is much lower, at most 0.01 in certain scenarios. Based on our results, we recommend implementing additional security measures to protect SRL models from malicious attacks. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of evaluating the effectiveness of SRL models against a wide range of potential threats, rather than just those with no knowledge. Finally, based on our findings, we suggest simple techniques that can help reduce the impact of attacks against SRL models, including data augmentation via noise injection and training against a diverse set of artificial adversaries. We believe that our research provides the most comprehensive assessment of SRL model vulnerability to date. As far as our knowledge goes, this study represents the deepest examination of vulnerabilities in speech representation learning models performed for any speech technology application. The code used in our experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/alexgalewski/srl-attack. In our research, we've introduced a way to incorporate the E-value into the causal inference process, particularly when dealing with missing data. This is achieved through incorporating the E-value into the inverse probability treatment weight (IPTW) method. The proposed IPTW-EV approach weights each subject based on the E-value of their observed data, enabling better model fit and robustness. As a result, IPTW-EV produces more reliable estimates and confidence intervals that are less susceptible to assumptions about missingness. Furthermore, our method allows for the evaluation of how robust causal conclusions are to the choice of model for dealing with missing data. By applying our approach to eight datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, over various missing data scenarios, our results demonstrate the benefits of incorporating the E-value into the analysis. In particular, our estimates and confidence intervals exhibited minimal or no dependence on the model chosen for handling missing data, and showed improved accuracy and narrower confidence intervals compared to the traditional IPTW approach. This is an adaptation of past work focusing on binary outcomes and multiple imputation, with our version also producing reliable results in the presence of covariate effect modification and higher levels of missing data. Consequently, our findings suggest the use of IPTW-EV as a robust and reliable method for estimating causal effects even in complex data scenarios. Lastly, our software enables the easy implementation of IPTW-EV for estimating causal effects with missing data. This is facilitated through a R package named 'ipow', where the E-value approach can be easily replicated from the provided examples. We then derive the explicit form of the corresponding $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ representations for both categories. Furthermore, we propose a basis for the quantum plane representations that exhibit well-defined, lower-order Casimir action. As a consequence, we provide explicit forms for the eigenspaces of the higher-order Casimir operators. Moreover, we establish a basis for the space of solutions to the quantum Yang-Baxter equation in a manner consistent with the Poincaré group. In addition, we show how the subspaces of tensor products of quantum planes can be described as representations of the monoid of shifted quantum planes. Finally, we provide a explanation of the emergence of tachyon from the limit of a shifted quantum plane representation. These results have potential applications in the open string theory on a BTZ black hole background. They can also be used to study a two-dimensional system involving grapes and strings via a gauge equivalence transformation related to the q-deformation of the Virasoro algebra. Such a gauge equivalence transformation is itself a consequence of the 1/2-deformation of the algebra of classical Weyl operators. The theorems we established for the quantum plane are also valid in the context of the extended quantum plane, which involves an additional variable, and are relevant to the study of boundary conditions in the theory. In the theory, the boundary conditions can be viewed as a type II Frobenius algebra structure on the homogeneous space $\mathrm{AdS}_2$, whereas the extended quantum plane is relevant to a related type I Frobenius algebra structure on $\mathrm{AdS}_2$. A second appendix establishes a connection with the literature via a gauge equivalence transformation related to the group of unitary elements with absolute value 1 in $\mathbb{C}^2$ and a q-deformation of $\mathrm{SU}_q(2)$.

The incorrect use of cryptographic functions, such as hashing and encryption, occurs frequently across various platforms, placing programs and their users at risk. By analyzing how developers interact with cryptographic libraries in different languages - Python, Java, and C - we strive to understand what leads to misuse. Our research method involves creating modified versions of crypto libraries in each language with varying complexities of API designs. We then presented these modified libraries to a group of programmers who performed simple tasks, such as checking digital signatures, as part of a mock scenario. Our findings indicate that the way crypto functions are accessed and the level of feedback provided by these functions significantly contribute to the frequency of misuse. Additionally, we found that the frequency of misuse varies significantly between programming in different languages, with hash functions being the most frequently misused crypto functions across all languages, and programmers often misuse these functions by incorrect usage of the function itself, rather than providing incorrect input. Lastly, we discovered several potential strategies that crypto library developers, programmers, and educators could implement to reduce the frequency of misuse of crypto functions. Our work contributes to the understanding of a critical security threat at the application level, enabling the development of more effective methods for preventing misuse of crypto functions. It also offers recommendations for improving the safety of digital transactions and the security of programs at the application level. Our research resources are accessible at https://misuse-crypto.github.io.

We derive a novel limit theorem that indicates the convergence of a series of valid demand sequences can result in a similar convergence of series of cost functions, but in an opposite and often conflicting manner. This outcome presents a challenge to previous theories that aimed to utilize demand functions to determine equilibrium outcomes in economic models. Our research implies that even though the sequence of demands converges to a well-defined demand function, it does not provide enough information to accurately determine the resulting equilibrium price. Crucially, our findings reveal that the set of feasible prices which can be equilibria under varying non-linear pricing functions has no defined boundary, and can be composed of an infinite sequence of distinct prices. Additionally, the consequences of our results for understanding the limits of economic models that feature changing or dynamic demand responses are also explored. They suggest that even though the sequence of demands converges to a consistent demand function, the model's behavior appears to diverge from its previous patterns of activity. In a collaborative effort, Balasco et al. (2021) previously established a similar limit theorem but restricted their analysis to a specific subset of valid demands, and our research extends their findings to a broader class of demands while retaining the same assumptions regarding the presence of a single convergent demands sequence and a corresponding sequence of non-linear pricing functions. They also recently contributed to an improvement to our analysis that broadened the application of Balasco et al.'s (2021) results, and our findings now hold for a class of models with the possibility of the absence of a balanced general equilibrium. They achieved this by relaxing one of the conditions that led to the convergence of Balasco et al.' 2021's results; namely, the requirement that the model must have a unique balanced general equilibrium. They showed that this condition can be replaced with a more realistic assumption that the model is stable and does not experience infinite consumption or savings. They further utilized this revised analysis to verify that a recently proposed model of the US economy, the New Keynesian Sticky Price Mold, does not exhibit the phenomenon of the convergence of demands leading to a conflict between the sequence of costs and prices. They discovered that this phenomenon is prevented by assuming the model's presence of a balanced general equilibrium and the presence of a monotonically increasing concave production technology. To eliminate adverse effects caused by noise in variational quantum algorithms, researchers employ mitigation strategies based on repeated circuit evaluations. A popular approach is the randomized Pauli method, effective in determining ground states but whose efficacy diminishes for excited states. We've revised our mitigation scheme to counteract the most dominant noise sources affecting VQE, specifically white-noise fluctuations in two key aspects: multiple circuit evaluations and quantum state preparation. Our enhanced method achieves a substantial speedup, with results demonstrating a notable enhancement in convergence rates of the variational quantum eigensector algorithm when applied in combination with quantum signal processing. The improved scheme yields a significant decrease in the required number of circuit evaluations, offering a promising solution for managing noise in VQE. We've validated our findings using the IBM quantum simulator to compute the energy eigenvalues of the $\rm{H}_2$ molecule. Our experiments show that the modified scheme significantly accelerates the VQE convergence process without relying on classical signal processing techniques. The implementation details are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/yo-saki/white_noise Mitigation_for_VQE. We believe our work will serve as a foundation for future research on mitigation strategies to help advance the development of quantum algorithms resistant to noise. Furthermore, the developed code offers a useful building block for executing noise mitigation schemes in real-world quantum computing environments. VILT successfully improved the connection between text and image meanings by incorporating visual cues into a transformer encoder. However, its teacher-guided pretraining strategy restricts the ability of the decoder to use visual guidance for image generation. Therefore, this research expands upon the VILT approach by adopting a contrastive pretraining method that increases visual guidance in the decoder. Additionally, CVLT+ improves text-guidance in the encoder by utilizing a conditional feature map generated from the decoder's visual guidance. Evaluation of CVLT+ on the image text localization task showed its superiority over the original VILT approach. Furthermore, renovations to the image-text pair matching pipeline and the adoption of an image-text ranking loss helped minimize pretraining biases. This research also introduced the Visual-guided Multi-adversarial Imitation Networks (VMAIN) approach, targeting the imitation learning of text-based image generation. Based on the CVLT+ backbone, VMAIN uses a conditional feature map to guide the matching of conditional features in the generator and inverse mapping, enabling more realistic imitation learning of text-based image generation. According to the evaluation results, VMAIN showed significant improvements over the existing approach. This research contributed a new dataset called Ganit, consisting of 1,500 pairs of real images and generated scenes, for the purpose of evaluating the imitation learning of text-based image generation. The proposed CVLT+ method and the new VMAIN approach are available on the GitHub platform. In addition, the new dataset Ganit can be accessed at https://github.com/njru-ilm-group/Ganit. The evaluation results of the original VILT method can be found at https://github.com/njru-ilm-group/CVLT. The dicompyler++ and highdicom libraries enhance the development of medical imaging analytics by facilitating data/experiment reproduction, collaborative research, and compatible data storage, allowing for the seamless integration of machine learning models across different institutions and software tools. By standardizing data and processing methods, these libraries accelerate the analysis pipeline and empower users to run previously created experiments with novel data sources, thereby promoting reproducibility and knowledge sharing. Highdicom particularly excels in reading, writing, and transforming DICOM files while providing access to their associated metadata, while dicompyler++ offers tools for image/information reconstruction, compression, and communication, as well as medical volume rendering capabilities. By utilizing highdicom's reading, parsing, and writing functions, users can convert images into a unified format suitable for analysis, and in return, dicompyler++ can reconstruct the original compressed data. Furthermore, the libraries' modular structure allows for the easy adaptation of one library's components to third-party projects, promoting a unified medical imaging data ecosystem. As examples of the libraries' utility, we illustrate how highdicom is used in streamlining the pre-processing of small animal CT datasets, and how dicompyler++ is employed in the development of a cloud-based pipeline for distributing uncompressed CT data. Overall, the utilization of highdicom and dicompyler++ in medical imaging analytics is encouraged to ensure compatibility, reproducibility, and efficient data management. These libraries are available for public use under the terms of the GNU General Public License v3.0 at https://mattbat.com/highdicom/ and https://mattbat.com/dicompyler++/. Ongoing projects include the development of highdicom for adapting MRI data and futures for DICOM-based document parsing. As the primary maintainer of highdicom, we welcome contributions from the community to further develop these libraries in the service of reproducible medical imaging analytics. In particular, potential additions could focus on enhancing support for modern imaging standards like MRI, providing access to standardized diagnostic information, and integrating interfaces for popular diagnostic tools such as 3D slicer and PyMED. In conclusion, the widespread adoption of highdicom and dicompyler++ is crucial for achieving interoperability in medical imaging analytics, and we encourage the continued development of these libraries by the community to ensure a unified data ecosystem. These libraries are available for public use and public contributions are invited at https://mattbat.com/highdicom/ and https://mattbat.com/dicompyler

The significance of DNA sequences is often represented by their word signatures, which contain valuable information explaining how DNA classification tasks function. Unfortunately, word signatures are typically hidden from human understanding, making it difficult to interpret how they relate to established scientific knowledge. In this research, we investigated whether we can omit the complex DNA encoding process and directly learn signatures from DNA sequences to improve their interpretability. We achieved this through a novel signature learning approach called DNAJet, which translates DNA into a unified representation suitable for signature discovery. Our method allows signatures to be expressed as causally related features in a linear model, providing interpretability similar to word signatures in language analysis. We conducted experiments on multiple datasets and observed that DNAJet signatures consistently reflected the underlying DNA causal structure. Moreover, the signatures obtained by DNAJet possessed superior explanatory power in tumor classification tasks compared to state-of-the-art techniques that analyze DNA word signatures. Interestingly, the signatures obtained by DNAJet related to existing scientific knowledge in certain domains but also highlighted novel connections, such as the causal role of CG reversals in cancer development. Our results indicate that DNAJet enhances our comprehension of how DNA functions at the molecular level. The source code of DNAJet has been made available. This phenomenon has significant implications for understanding charge transport and absorption of light in d- and f-electron systems, particularly in materials such as high-temperature superconductors, heavy fermions, and actinide compounds. By analyzing the absorption process, we observe that in the vicinity of a Mott transition, the weight of charge excitations is distributed across a very broad energy range, with the majority of weight residing at high energies far beyond the bounds of the absorption band. This behavior manifests as a vast continuum of spectral weight, which can be characterized by a scale of energy of the order of U, the strength of correlation. This concept challenges the conventional idea that spectral weight is primarily associated with low-energy excitations, and instead suggests a profound link between high-energy and low-energy properties of strongly correlated materials, with the former governing the critical fluctuations that facilitate the transition. As a result, conventional descriptions based on phase diagrams in terms of the correlation length may need to be supplemented with a new parameter, the high-energy fluctuation scale, for accurate descriptions of critical behavior and quantum fluctuations. A novel approach has been developed that efficiently solves implicit time approximations in systems of conservation laws, which often arise in kinetic models. The method builds on the Q1c-Q1b method used for explicit timesteps, but is extended to accommodate non-linear solenoidal equations using an implicit Euler scheme. The linear system resulting from the finite element discretization can be efficiently solved by introducing internal degrees of freedom and approximating a weighted, extended Lagrange multiplier. The solution of the linear system is well-conditioned, albeit with a increased cost that scales as $N^2$ compared to an assemblage operator with a matrix-free implementation that requires $N$ operations. The approach has been successfully tested for a broad range of problems including the Landau-Lifshitz equation, the Baer-Nash equations, the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook equation and the Extended Poincaré equation for $Q$-tensor systems. The landau-lifshitz equation example showed that the approach can achieve a precise solution with a temporal accuracy of order 1/N. The approach has been implemented with a matrix-free solver and a sparse solver for the linear system, but is actually more efficient than expected when using a matrix-free solver, as the linear system is well-conditioned. The approach has been tested for a broad range of problems and shows a temporal accuracy of order 1/N. We introduce Landmark Gabor Filters, a novel image representation method built on a landmark-based architecture. LGFs are generated by combining multiple Gabor filters centered over predefined landmark locations. This approach capitalizes on the unique properties of Gabor filters in encoding diverse image details and exploits their collective robustness when faced with various orientations. By incorporating landmarks, LGFs are able to maintain consistent and precise representations of images under different orientation conditions. This results in landmark-based Gabor filters outperforming traditional Gabor filters in numerous orientation scenarios. This research marks the first comprehensive analysis of MiSO orbits and their feasibility in satellite constellations. It showcases a demonstrated concept that can alleviate the congestion in low-Earth orbit caused by increasing satellite densities. The study finds that implementing MiSO orbits in geostationary orbits can result in significant propellant reductions, suggesting their potential application in future satellite systems. This research highlights the benefits of MiSO orbits and encourages their integration in the design of satellite constellations. In the field of explainable recommendation systems, researchers have suggested that features like post-hoc explanations can enhance the trustworthiness of recommendation models by making their decision-making processes understandable to end-users. Unlike internal explanations that aim to mimic the model's internal workings, post-hoc explanations are external features that can be understood by humans. Previous studies on post-hoc explanations in recommendation models have been limited, and most existing explanations in the literature have been uncritical, meaning they do not influence the model's performance and can often provide misleading information to users. This study examines the effect of uncertain post-hoc explanations on the reliability of recommendation models. A novel, human-centric explanation technique called CUE explains by measuring how well an explanation aligns with true items that are liked by users. We discovered that when users are provided with uncertain explanations that are either accurate or inaccurate regarding their personal preferences, the model's reliability decreases compared to the baseline model without explanations. Additionally, the accuracy of the model is not negatively affected. This study demonstrates that when users do not require it, the reliance of recommendation models on post-hoc explanations increases errors. Furthermore, the error rate of models using explanations provided by a language model significantly decreases compared to the model initially assigned to the user. We speculate that using uncertain explanations may cause the model to rely more heavily on user-specific datasets, leading to increased errors. We provide these findings along with additional insights in our pre-print paper, as well as open-source code and a user-specific dataset at https://github.com/GeekFuerst/eXplain. Our work will be presented at the 14th Conference on Information Systems for Designer at ACM RecSys '24. A extended version of this study is also published at Journal of Intelligent Information Systems. A video overview of this work can be seen at YouTube. We have conducted direct imaging observations of the young star AU Mic in the near ultraviolet as part of a search for exoplanets. The system was observed using the Giant Magellan Telescope's AO system, GOUGE, in two different filters, its native UV band at 364 nm, and in the 670 nm band. AU Mic's b-planetary-mass exoplanet was detected in both bands, revealing a mass loss through its atmosphere that synchronizes with its 10-day stellar flares. The atmospheric loss was estimated to be in the range of 10^11 electrons per second in quiescence, increasing to 10^14 electrons per second during flares. This loss results in a stream of charged particles that has been accreted by the planet. We have calculated that for AU Mic b to maintain its current mass over 100 million years, it must have accreted matter at least ten times the mass of Jupiter each decade during its lifetime. This rate of accretion far exceeds typical accretion levels following a planet's formation, presenting a puzzle. We have considered two possible explanations: the planet could be engaging with disk-based material that has yet to be captured by its atmosphere, or the planet may be engaging in a highly eccentric orbit with its host star, periodically engaging with stellar material during close approaches. This rare opportunity to observe an exoplanet during a stellar flare may provide key evidence to support either theory. AU Mic's system was also found to contain a possible signal indicating the presence of a massive object, possibly a additional planetary-mass exoplanet, although this indication is tentative and requires confirmation. KNN, SVM, and several neural network models were tested for their ability to withstand extreme class imbalance situations. Our results showed that while deep neural networks are capable of withstanding severe class imbalance, shallower neural network models are more heavily affected. In contrast, KNN and SVM are severely impacted by severe class imbalance. Furthermore, the effectiveness of oversampling, undersampling, and threshold adjustment techniques vary significantly depending on the algorithm used. Notably, when dealing with severe class imbalance, oversampling consistently performs better than threshold adjustment, while undersampling performs better than oversampling in situations of extreme imbalance. The insights from our research will inform the practical application of machine learning models to real-world datasets. Additionally, the algorithms and metrics utilized in our research have been published online for others to build upon.

- KNN and SVM are notably affected by severe class imbalance in comparison to neural networks, which can withstand severe imbalance.
- The performance impacts of using various oversampling, undersampling, and threshold adjustment techniques vary significantly depending on the algorithm used.
- When dealing with severe class imbalance, oversampling tends to outperform threshold adjustment, while undersampling performs better than oversampling in situations of extreme imbalance.

Evaluating gravitational forces between numerous small bodies in astrophysical scenarios like galaxy and planet formation can be computationally expensive. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) offers an effective solution by reducing O(N^2) computations to nearly O(N) with the aid of approximations and data organization, although this still poses a challenge for simulations involving very large N. The Graves-Faust FMM implementation presented here exhibits high performance and efficiency, thanks to optimizations using GPU-based architectures. In standard benchmarks, the code displays a smooth progression from serial to parallel and FMM computations. In a typical cosmological simulation with N = 512^3, implementing FMM yields a 6-fold speedup compared to the straightforward force calculation and a 10-fold speedup compared to the already parallel Barnes-Hut algorithm. Furthermore, integrating FMM into a MAC tree-based method reveals that while it generally surpasses the latter in terms of accuracy, there are exceptional circumstances - such as extremely high resolutions or short timescales - where the tree-based approach might experience numerical instability, necessitating the use of an adaptive hybrid technique. A possible direction for enhancing FMM's accuracy in such scenarios involves leveraging the Relaxed Error Correction. An initial examination indicates that this could enhance the accuracy of the tree-based approach and reduce the threshold for switching from FMM to the tree-based method, though further investigation is necessary. Ultimately, the Graves-Faust FMM code reported here has the potential to greatly enhance the efficiency of gravitational computations and should find immediate use in astrophysical simulations. Furthermore, its high performance and flexibility make it an attractive choice for researchers to incorporate into their own astrophysical simulation software frameworks. The code is freely available for download at https://github.com/GravesFaust/FMM. We propose a novel experimental approach to detect a specific process where a visible sector neutralino disintegrates into a hidden sector neutralino and an energetic gamma ray, which is a distinct signature of a missing massive neutrino (MMN) dark matter model. This signature, characterized by a single gamma ray emanating from a distant galaxy or cluster, will be identifiable at the upcoming CTA observatory, whose high sensitivity will enable the detection of extremely rare decays, even with a massive neutrino mass of 100 GeV. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough assessment of a mathematical model that connects the strength of an exotic interaction to the decay of a neutrino into a gamma ray and a hidden sector neutrino. This analysis, derived from the model's features, is comprised of two primary components: the rate of decay and the dispersion pattern of energy. We provide precise mathematical expressions for these components and confirm their accuracy through the study of a representative dark matter model. Finally, we explore the potential for the CTA observatory to detect this decay using the CTA Figures of Merit, establishing a relationship between the total cross-section of an exotic interaction and the neutrino mass in the process. This research indicates that the CTA observatory can detect the described decay for a massive neutrino mass of 100 GeV with a total cross-section of $10^{-1}$ pb GeV and a Majorana mass of 50 GeV. Additionally, we demonstrate that the CTA observatory can detect the described decay for a massive neutrino mass of 1 GeV with a significantly higher total cross-section of $10^{-5}$ pb GeV, but only at higher energies above 100 TeV. These findings will be made available under a free open-access license. The proposed research will be conducted as an experiment at the CTA observatory and the results will be studied in relation to the impact of sub-pico-eV masses of light bosons on the Hubble constant's value. Furthermore, we outline potential future research pathways in the field, including examining how the described decay might be detected at high-energy colliders and testing the constraints of this particular dark matter model compared to its broader applications in the hidden sector. Ultimately, this comprehensive analysis of the described decay serves as a model case for the broader field of dark matter particle physics at detectors. The Sinkhorn algorithm, an efficient method for solving the Schrödinger problem via entropic regularization, has limitations when it comes to incoherent or unregularizable instances: it collapses to zero or cycles indefinitely without providing a solution. New modified algorithms have been developed to overcome these issues, building on the Gottlieb-Liu technique and introducing a balanced approach to minimize and maximize the regularized problem's objective function. These algorithms demonstrate improved convergence properties and regularizability compared to the original Sinkhorn algorithm, as seen in coherent and incoherent instances. Additionally, our analysis highlights the relationship between our methods and a coherent version of the gradient projection algorithm, with the proposed methods offering faster convergence rates in many cases. Our findings also illustrate the importance of the algorithmic stopping criterion, particularly for incoherent instances, and demonstrate the yE.col(S) scalability of the proposed methods on real-world applications. Furthermore, our analysis provides a fundamental contribution by establishing a connection between the limit points of the regularized problem and its unconditional convergence for arbitrary values of the regularization parameter. This has significant implications for a broad range of algorithms, including Sneller-Schönhofen, AggreSzeged, and their unregularized counterparts. To facilitate reproducibility, our research code is available for public access at https://github.com/Tassillo/Regularized-Schrödinger-Problems. As an example of its utility, our reduced-incoherence algorithm can be utilized to create a minimum entanglement structure for a specific four-qubit state, with our approach offering faster convergence rates in this application. By doing so, FSMSN demonstrates the ability to model complex phenomena like phase transformations in materials and flowing materials in an implicit manner, thereby expanding the practical application of fully implicit methods in computational mechanics and physics. Our study shows that the FSMSN approach generally experiences a substantial reduction of computational time, with computation times oscillating between being two to three hundred times lower or higher compared to conventional methods depending on the specific problem at hand. Our experimental findings further indicate that the choice of initial conditions and multi-step schemes can significantly influence computational efficiency. For modeling phase transformations in materials, four distinct multi-step schemes yielded distinct results, while modeling flowing materials revealed the importance of scheme selection in maintaining solution accuracy. Our research reveals that the FSMSN approach promises considerable promise in enhancing computational speed and efficiency. However, its broad effectiveness is contingent upon the specific problem at hand, with certain test cases showcasing decreased performance compared to conventional methods. In this research, we conducted studies to understand the impact of sharing a robot's task-related information with humans. We discovered that when humans are shown the robot's data, it actually reduces their productivity, but if they are also shown that the robot is making decisions, then revealing the data actually improves their efficiency. We propose HiTMap, an extension of the metric exploration model that enables efficient navigation even in environments with uncertain distortions. HiTMap's key strength lies in its ability to maintain minimal overall distortion during map construction, resulting in significant navigation cost savings. In contrast to traditional global metric maps like Cartography's, HiTMap's approach embodies a local mapping philosophy, where a robot's perceived environment is broken down into smaller components to account for spatial uncertainty. Furthermore, HiTMap's implementation boasts computational efficiency, facilitating its practical use in real-time robot navigation. We have conducted comprehensive simulations, including various 2D and 3D scenarios, to compare HiTMap's performance with existing navigation methods, and the results clearly demonstrate its advantages. Moreover, we have successfully deployed HiTMap on a mobile robot to assess its real-world effectiveness. Our experiments show that HiTMap's maps exhibit a notable improvement in geometric accuracy and reduced navigation errors compared to the random mapping strategy. Importantly, HiTMap's local mapping paradigm allows for the integration of sparse loops and minimal reprojection errors to create more accurate maps. These findings suggest that HiTMap represents a viable and efficient solution for robust and reliable navigation in environments with uncertain distortions. With its potential for application in both terrestrial and aerial robots, HiTMap represents a suitable option for use in various navigation scenarios. This research paper explores an innovative development in creating a 2-D Z-complementary array code set (ZCACS) with the ability to simultaneously transmit two distinct data sets, addressing a long-standing challenge in this field. Unlike conventional approaches using generalized Boolean functions, our proposed solution utilizes restricted sum functions consisting of restricted sums, offering enhanced flexibility and the potential for improved code performance. The paper establishes the conditions under which the resulting code sets will have optimal density properties. Additionally, we present two strategies for generating the restricted sum functions needed to construct the optimal ZCACS. One method utilizes cyclic shifts to create these functions, while the other employs linear cyclic Boolean functions. Furthermore, we develop a method for directly translating the optimal restricted sum functions into optimal ZCACS, showcasing the interconnections between restricted sum functions, cyclic shifts, linear cyclic Boolean functions, and ZCACS. Our investigation ultimately yields an algorithm to construct an optimal two-dimensional ZCACS with size $L_{N_1,N_2}=(N_1-1)(N_2-1)+1$, for given prime numbers $N_1$ and $N_2$ exceeding 2. To verify the efficacy of this novel algorithm, we carry out a comparative analysis of the code arrays it produces with existing one-dimensional general $m$-sequence code sets of lengths $N_1$ and $N_2$. Our findings confirm that these code sets possess superior density properties, while noting that existing solutions require additional processes to achieve density optimization. Lastly, this paper discusses the potential applications of the ZCACS in data transmission and proposes two innovative schemes, blind one-bit and one-bit powered massive-MIMO, showcasing the promise of the ZCACS in addressing contemporary challenges. One of these schemes uses the ZCACS to achieve half-dollarized coverage, while the other leverages the ZCACS to accomplish Z-complementary coverage, thus contributing to the development of new techniques in this field. Moreover, we present a new approach to constructing a pair of complementary arrays using the ZCACS, achieving a unique property where the intersection of the two arrays consists of a single symbol. This finding offers a new possibility for constructing differentiable arrays. Specifically, by using the constructed pair, we can build a unique two-dimensional array with the desired property. The application, implemented as a web page, allows users to interact with a time graph by dragging and rotating it, observing how its transformations influence associated rank and size plots. This study concludes with a discussion on the challenges associated with developing these connected visualizations, focusing particularly on the difficulties of accurately mapping regions of interest in time graphs to entities in rank and size plots. In the realm of Electronic Health Records (EHR), a network-like structure naturally emerges due to the diverse links between patients and medical entities. Consequently, a range of deep graph learning methods have been adopted for various tasks, such as patient similarity calculation and disease prediction. However, these approaches face several challenges, including sparse and imbalanced data. Furthermore, patient data often contains sensitive information, necessitating confidentiality measures. To address these concerns, a new heterogeneous graph neural network has been developed, which first consolidates the structural information within patient profiles, then leverages the propagated attention to balance the data based on profile strengths, finally incorporating attention to enable the exploration of neighbor-based representation. Our proposed approach excels existing methods by achieving significant improvements in disease prediction tasks on several real-world EHR datasets. For instance, when predicting the presence of coronary heart disease, our model achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.8203, outperforming the current state-of-the-art model with a 0.0263 improvement in accuracy.
